1.1 Conventions

We follow the normalizations of [SGPT]:

5.24 Maxima and the maximum principle

For a function $f$, we write $f^*(x)=\limsup _{y\to x}f(y)$ for its upper semicontinuous regularization. A subset of a complex manifold is pluripolar if each of its points has a neighborhood $U$ such that the part of the subset in $U$ is contained in $\{ p=-\infty \} $ for some $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$. The local upper-envelope theorem recalled in [SGPT] states that if a nonempty family of plurisubharmonic functions is locally uniformly bounded above, then the regularization of its supremum is plurisubharmonic and differs from the supremum only on a pluripolar set.

5.25 Normalized compactness

Fix a smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$, used for $L^1$ norms. Consider a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on a connected domain that is locally uniformly bounded above. By the local compactness theorem recalled in [SGPT], it has a subsequence that either converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ or converges locally uniformly to $-\infty $. For normalized $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$, a point at which the maximum is attained excludes the second alternative, and connectedness of $X$ propagates the first one across $X$.

5.27 Local products and capacity

Bedford–Taylor products of bounded plurisubharmonic functions, and the capacity defined through them, measure the exceptional sets of plurisubharmonic functions and control bounded approximation. We recall these classical facts of local pluripotential theory from [SGPT, GZ17]. The plurifine topology is the coarsest topology that makes all local plurisubharmonic functions continuous. It is finer than the ordinary topology; in particular, strict superlevel sets of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions are plurifine open.

5.27 Local products and capacity

Both are classical results of local pluripotential theory [Chapters 3 and 4, GZ17]; the conventions for bounded products and capacity in [Chapter 2, SGPT] agree with these up to fixed constants.

5.27 Local products and capacity

A function is quasi-continuous if, for every $\epsilon >0$, it is continuous outside an open set of capacity less than $\epsilon $. Plurisubharmonic functions have this property for the local Bedford–Taylor capacity, and a Borel set has zero capacity if and only if it is pluripolar. A locally uniformly bounded monotone sequence of plurisubharmonic functions converges in capacity: to its limit if it decreases, and to the upper semicontinuous regularization of its limit if it increases. If uniformly bounded plurisubharmonic functions converge in capacity, their local products converge weakly, and this remains true after the products are multiplied by uniformly bounded quasi-continuous coefficients converging in capacity. These local results, recalled in [SGPT, GZ17], also apply to quasi-plurisubharmonic functions after a common smooth correction.

5.27 Local products and capacity

The comparison principle of Bedford and Taylor also has mixed forms, recalled in [SGPT]. 5.27 Local products and capacity

The gradient term, and its products with positive Bedford–Taylor factors of bounded potentials, are nonnegative. These identities belong to the bounded local calculus recalled in [SGPT, GZ17]; they follow by decreasing regularization, and bounded potentials have the local Sobolev regularity needed to define the gradient term. In particular, inequalities derived from this formula survive local smoothing with a lower curvature error tending to zero.

5.34.2 Lelong level sets

Siu's analyticity theorem states that, for every quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ and every $c>0$, the upper level set $\{ x:\nu (u,x)\geq c\} $ is an analytic subset. After a smooth local correction, this is the theorem for closed positive currents, which we use in the form recalled in [SGPT]; see section 25.2 for the original source.

5.36 The global curvature bound

This is the form of [Theorem 14.12, DemAM11] used in this book. The local generators in the construction are the weighted Bergman generators of $\mathcal I(mu)$; smooth local corrections do not change this ideal. On overlaps the local Bergman sums are comparable, so the glued logarithm keeps the analytic type $(1/m,\mathcal I(mu))$. The construction freezes the continuous lower bound $\gamma $ on sufficiently small coordinate balls, and its curvature error combines the modulus of continuity of $\gamma $ with an overlap term that tends to zero as $m$ increases. It is this global curvature estimate, and not merely the local convergence of proposition 5.35.1, that we take from the theorem.

We also use the regularization of closed currents in the form recalled in [SGPT]. 5.37 Multiplier ideals and logarithmic poles

For a logarithmic pole along a submanifold, weighted integrability of a holomorphic germ is determined by its vanishing order in the normal directions. For general singularities, the valuative characterization of multiplier ideals and the strong openness theorem, both recalled in [SGPT], make the comparison of multiplier ideals compatible with maxima, sums and increasing limits.

5.38 Lelong numbers and divisorial estimates

We use the following local consequence of Siu's decomposition theorem, recalled in [SGPT] and [DemAM11]. If $T$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current and $E$ is a prime divisor, the restriction of (the coefficient measures of) $T$ to $E$ equals the generic Lelong number of $T$ along $E$ times $[E]$. In particular, removing finitely many of these divisorial components from $T$ leaves a positive current. Distinct prime divisors do not contribute overlapping mass, since their intersections have codimension at least two. All these are local statements about closed currents.

Lemma 5.38.8

Every point of the smaller ball is the center of a Euclidean ball of a fixed radius contained in the intermediate ball. The local Lelong monotonicity formula, recalled in [SGPT], bounds the Lelong number at this center by a fixed multiple of the trace mass of the intermediate ball. The finite cover gives one bound on $Z$. Since smooth additions and additive constants do not change Lelong numbers, this proves the assertion for the original potentials. $\square$

5.41.4 Pointwise Legendre transforms

The minimum principle can also show that a supremum is already upper semicontinuous. For a concave family of potentials, the regularized Legendre transform is a potential on a product. The minimum principle identifies its inverse transforms with the original family everywhere, and applying the one-variable duality once more identifies the regularization with the pointwise supremum. We first state this duality precisely, including its behavior at the endpoints; the general Legendre–Fenchel theorem is recalled in [appendix on convex analysis, SGPT].

Lemma 5.46.4

Proof. On a small coordinate ball, take plurisubharmonic local potentials $a,b$ with $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ and $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b$, by [Chapter III, Proposition 1.19, p. 135, DemCADG]. Put $h=a-b\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The trace identity gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \eta ^{n-1}=0$ in the sense of distributions. Dividing by the smooth positive volume form $\eta ^ n$ gives a scalar second-order operator with smooth coefficients whose principal matrix is a positive multiple of the inverse of the Hermitian matrix of $\eta $; it is uniformly elliptic on every smaller ball. Local elliptic regularity therefore makes $h$ smooth. Thus $T-S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ is smooth and carried by a Lebesgue null set, so its coefficient measures vanish. This proves equality locally, and hence globally. $\square$

18.4.7 Analytic and divisorial singularities

For a potential $a$ with analytic singularities, the multiplier-ideal order controls the ordinary order: by lemma 5.38.11, every quasi-plurisubharmonic $v$ with $v\preceq _{\mathcal I}a$ satisfies $v\preceq a$. The ideal envelope of $a$ is then a competitor for its ordinary envelope, and the two envelopes coincide. This extends [Proposition 3.2.10, SGPT] to smooth backgrounds.

Theorem 18.6.4

Let $Y$ be a compact connected Riemann surface and $\theta $ a smooth positive form of total mass one. Fix a smooth positive probability volume form on $Y$, again denoted by $\mathrm{d}V$, and use $\mathcal K_\theta $, the envelopes and the ideal metric on $Y$ in place of $X$. Then the ideal models with finitely many logarithmic poles and zero non-pluripolar mass are dense in $\mathcal K_\theta $ for the $L^1$ topology. The logarithmic coefficients can be chosen rational, so these approximants have analytic singularities in the convention of [SGPT]. Consequently the completion in proposition 18.6.1 is all of $\mathcal K_\theta $, and the metric on ideal classes is not complete.

19.9.5 The body of a graded section algebra

We use the following semigroup counting theorem, recalled in [Theorem C.2.1, SGPT]. Let $r\geq 0$, and let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb Z^{r+1}$ be an additive semigroup that generates $\mathbb Z^{r+1}$ as a group and lies in a closed convex cone in $\mathbb R^ r\times \mathbb R_{\geq 0}$ whose height-one slice is compact and whose only point at height zero is the origin. Then the number of points of $\Sigma $ at height $m$, divided by $m^ r$, converges to the Euclidean volume of the height-one slice of the closed convex cone generated by $\Sigma $.

20.4.9 Bott–Chern classes and closed currents

Bott–Chern cohomology records a closed $(1,1)$-current modulo $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of global functions, and so separates the smooth background of the current from its potential. When $\theta $ is closed, subtracting the trace current from the pulled-back background gives a residual class on each model, and compatibility with pushforward organizes these classes into a b-divisor class in the sense of [section The notion of b-divisors, SGPT].

20.4.9 Bott–Chern classes and closed currents

When the models are Kähler, the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma identifies this cohomology with the real $(1,1)$-cohomology used in [section The notion of b-divisors, SGPT], and the definition agrees with the one given there.

16.29.12 Changes of representative and limiting mass

For closed backgrounds on a compact Kähler manifold, [chapter “Non-Archimedean pluripotential theory”, section “The definition of non-Archimedean metrics”, SGPT] indexes such systems by Kähler perturbations, as above, and defines their volume as a limit of the masses of the initial potentials. Its components are general test curves fixed by the ideal envelope, with initial potentials of positive mass, whereas our curves are constant on a prescribed left half-line and our system spaces impose no mass condition. For nonclosed positive backgrounds, the corresponding limit of masses is not invariant under the gauge bijections.

9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces

We use three facts about unibranch spaces. Resolutions and common smooth refinements of two resolutions exist, and a proper bimeromorphic map to a unibranch space has connected fibers [Theorems B.1.1–B.1.3, SGPT]. The Fornaess–Narasimhan criterion identifies plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ as the upper semicontinuous functions that are subharmonic on holomorphic disks [Theorem B.2.1, SGPT]. The ramified disk lift used below is the argument in [proof of Theorem B.2.2, SGPT].

25.1 Classical potentials, boundary problems, and capacity

25.1 Historical notes65E16F3944C7

Local regularization and products provide a common starting point for the results of this book. A smooth local correction makes these methods available for nonclosed backgrounds, including on Kähler manifolds. Global arguments must distinguish a closed class on a non-Kähler manifold from a nonclosed background: the former may lack the Kähler positivity used in classical existence theorems, while the latter loses the cohomological control of Monge–Ampère masses. Gauduchon duality, relative envelopes and the available mass bounds connect the sources discussed below. Their hypotheses also decide whether a solution keeps the ordinary singularity type of its reference or belongs only to its relative envelope class.

These notes identify the sources of the results of the book, with precise locators, and explain how the arguments given in the book relate to the original ones. Indications such as v1 or arXiv version in a locator refer to the version of the source that was used. Where needed, the conversion from the normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ or of the Chern–Ricci form used in a source to the conventions fixed at the beginning of the book is indicated next to the citation.

25.2 Plurisubharmonicity, currents, and singularities

25.2 Plurisubharmonic functions and regularizationE49C1A0D4682

Compactness, integrability and regularization are local properties, and they survive the passage to a nonclosed background because a quasi-plurisubharmonic function becomes plurisubharmonic after a smooth local correction. The $L^1$ compactness of normalized potentials in theorem 5.25.2, also stated by Dinew [Proposition 6.2, Dinew16], follows by propagating local compactness over a connected coordinate cover. Local exponential integrability, as recalled by Zeriahi [Section 1, Zeriahi01], becomes uniform over normalized potentials in lemma 5.26.2, through a contradiction argument with a weighted sum of potentials.

The comparison of convolutions in different coordinate charts in lemma 5.30.1, corollary 5.30.3 is the bounded part of the argument of Błocki and Kołodziej [§2, Lemmas 4–5, BK07]. Their full regularization theorem [Theorem 1, BK07] allows unbounded potentials and a positive continuous background. The proof of theorem 5.32.1 treats only the bounded case, which is all that the construction of products requires; it includes the extraction of a decreasing diagonal sequence and the rescaling that keeps the regularized forms strictly positive.

Demailly's regularization by the flow of the Chern connection [Theorem 4.1, Dem94] applies to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, where $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form: the theorem concerns a closed current with an arbitrary smooth lower bound, here $-\theta $, and this lower bound need not be closed. The monotonicity and logarithmic convexity of the regularization enter the estimate (5.42.11), whose linear error rate follows from the curvature inequality [Lemma 4.4, Dem94] and the expansion in [Proposition 3.8, equations (3.11), (4.3), and (4.5), Dem94]. In the present situation the curvature inequality needs neither a small $\epsilon $ term nor an $M_\epsilon $ correction, and local trace bounds make the constants uniform in the center and the radius.

The same expansion underlies the truncated Kiselman transform of lemma 5.42.1; see [Theorem 4.1 and Remark 4.7, Dem94] and Kołodziej–Nguyen [Lemma 4.1, KN19]. In lemma 5.42.4 the full base–fiber error is kept as a modulus tending to zero, and, as in [Remark 4.7, Dem94], a term linear in the radius absorbs the mixed and vertical errors. This formulation accommodates the unbounded potentials with finite $L^1$ norm that occur in theorem 15.8.1, where localizing the averaging radius makes the minimum-principle argument available away from the singular barrier.

For a continuous potential, the logarithmic derivative of the Chern averages tends to zero. Together with Dini's theorem and uniform continuity, this gives the uniform smooth approximation with vanishing curvature loss in lemma 5.42.5. For a Hölder reference, lemma 5.42.7 retains a common Hölder norm and rescales to genuine potentials. Dinh, Ma and Nguyên [Theorem 2.1, pp. 551–555, DMNFekete17] prove quantitative smooth regularization in a Kähler background using its local potentials. The proof here uses Chern averages and the continuous-potential curvature-loss estimate on the Hermitian background. Their quantitative Kähler estimate is not used.

Demailly's regularization in the form of theorem 5.36.5, whose approximants become divisorial with a smooth remainder after finitely many blowups, is the statement of Demailly and Păun [Theorem 3.2, DP04]. It allows an arbitrary smooth lower bound on a Hermitian manifold, and the smooth remainder after resolution is essential for its applications here. This sequence is in general different from the multiplier-ideal sequence of theorem 5.36.1, and we do not assume that a single sequence has the additional properties of both.

The analyticity of the sets where the Lelong number is at least $c>0$, recalled in 5.34.2 and used in lemma 12.19.4, theorem 11.8.1, is Siu's theorem [Main Theorem, p. 53, Siu74]; a smooth local correction makes it applicable to quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. The dimension bound for the Lelong level set and the existence of global irreducible components are stated in Demailly's book [Chapter III, Corollary 8.5, p. 174; Chapter II, Theorem 5.3, pp. 102–103, DemCADG]. The non-strict inequality is essential. In example 5.34.4, a summable series of line currents on the projective plane has the property that the set where the Lelong number exceeds one is a sequence of points accumulating at a point outside that set.

The closedness of polar curvature currents, proposition 5.46.7, is proved by the complete pluripolar restriction argument of Boucksom, Eyssidieux, Guedj and Zeriahi [author preprint v2, Theorem 1.8, Lemma 1.9 and Remark 1.10, BEGZ10]. The chain rule for bounded functions allows cutoffs that converge only pointwise, so the complete pluripolar set need not be closed, and a smooth local correction extends the argument to quasi-plurisubharmonic potentials with an arbitrary smooth background. Combined with the recovery of closed currents carried by a Lebesgue-null set from their traces, this removes the hypothesis that the pole set be closed from corollary 18.26.11, proposition 18.26.12. The simultaneous realization of the limiting currents is a separate question.

The Hausdorff estimate of corollary 5.34.3 follows from the Lelong mass formulas in Demailly's book [Chapter III, formulas (5.5)–(5.8), pp. 158–159, DemCADG] and holds in every positive bidimension. When a closed polar current vanishes outside an exceptional locus, the support theorem for currents carried by analytic sets [Chapter III, Corollaries 2.11 and 2.14, pp. 141–143, DemCADG] identifies the remaining divisorial part. Full local Monge–Ampère products at an unbounded locus of Hausdorff dimension zero rely instead on [Chapter III, Theorem 4.5 and Proposition 4.9, pp. 152–156, DemCADG], as stated in theorem 7.28.1. These products keep their top-degree mass on the pole set, whereas every lower-degree coefficient measure vanishes there. The local maximum argument of lemma 5.27.18 compares the residual measures and shows that they are invariant under bounded perturbations. Their global consequences for masses and models are discussed in section 25.3, section 25.4.

The local reference-integral estimate lemma 5.29.7 is related to the Hölder estimates for measure functionals of Dinh and Nguyên [arXiv v1, Lemma 3.5 and Proposition 3.6, pp. 9–10, DNHolder14]. Here the tests are bounded plurisubharmonic functions on nested balls. Keeping the cutoff-gradient terms gives a bound uniform in the Hölder norm of the reference; a finite cover yields corollary 5.29.9 for bounded tests with a common curvature lower bound.

The local moderation theorem of Dinh, Nguyên and Sibony [Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, pp. 466–467; proof pp. 468–471, DNSModerate10] gives exponential integrability with respect to locally moderate currents. The top-degree estimate lemma 5.29.10 follows here by applying the reference-integral estimate to consecutive truncations and absorbing their polynomial growth into the exponential tail. Guedj and Zeriahi's extremal-capacity comparison [Theorem 5.2, pp. 622–623, and Proposition 7.1, p. 632, GZIntrinsic05] motivates lemma 5.29.12. Its proof uses conservation of mass only for the closed Fubini–Study form on an auxiliary projective space. Local capacity comparison gives the Hermitian estimate proposition 5.29.13 with constants uniform for a common Hölder norm.

The convergence against a fixed non-pluripolar measure in lemma 5.44.2 rests on Cegrell's classical fixed-measure argument, which Kołodziej and Nguyen also state in a form allowing extraction of subsequences [Lemma 2.1 and Corollary 2.2, KN22]. Applying that statement to every subsequence gives convergence of the whole bounded sequence.

Let $f$ be a holomorphic function and $\chi $ a convex nondecreasing function. The sharp Sobolev criteria for the potentials $\chi (\log |f|)$ in 5.27.19 are due to Chen, Shao and Wang [v1, Theorems 1.1–1.2, pp. 2–3 and 19–22, CSW26]; their estimate in terms of the smallest multiplicity and their energy bound on small sublevel sets are [v1, Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 3.8, pp. 16–20, CSW26]. The proofs given here use the regularizations $\chi (\frac12\log (|f|^2+\varepsilon ^2))$, $\varepsilon >0$, to identify the weak gradient and to keep track of the residual divisor term in the distributional Laplacian, a term that the classical Laplacian omits. The power examples and their endpoint obstruction in example 5.27.23 are the calculation in normal coordinates and the table of [v1, Lemma 2.1 and Section 6.1, pp. 6–7 and 24–25, CSW26]. These local criteria for derivatives should not be confused with the theorem on products at a small unbounded locus discussed above.

The concentration example of proposition 5.27.30 is the point-mass case of Qin's [v1, Corollary 3.6, p. 14, QinLimits26]. Here the mass is computed directly from the transverse identity (5.27.29), which gives a smooth variant of the logarithmic truncation in [Lemma 2.4, pp. 9–10, QinLimits26]. The conclusion of lemma 5.27.27 for sequences with a common local bound agrees with [Proposition 7.2, p. 26, QinLimits26]; in the book it follows from the local range estimate proved earlier.

Theorem 5.27.35, which adds an arbitrary positive Radon measure to the Monge–Ampère measure of a fixed bounded potential in the limit, is Qin's [v1, Theorem B, p. 3, QinLimits26]. The addition along finitely many test functions and the passage to a determining family correspond to [Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 3.4, pp. 11–14, QinLimits26]. In the proof given here, the smooth ridge gives the limits of the lower-degree currents directly, finite iteration over atoms controls every mixed term, and the one-sided logarithmic bound also gives convergence in local capacity. The smoothness of the approximants is asserted for a smooth background, whereas Qin also treats continuous backgrounds.

The classification of vague cluster sets in theorem 5.27.38, according to which every vaguely closed set of positive measures is the full cluster set of a sequence of potentials tending to zero, is the case of the zero potential in [v1, Theorem A, pp. 2–3, QinLimits26]. The metric for the vague topology and the concatenation of dense sequences are [Lemma 3.3, p. 12 and Lemma 4.1, p. 14, QinLimits26], and the comparison example with moving measures is [Example B.1, p. 28, QinLimits26]. In the book, finite addition of atoms gives smooth approximants that converge in local capacity directly. The construction with moving measures over a fixed bounded background in theorem 5.27.41 also corresponds to [Theorem 3.4, pp. 13–14, QinLimits26]. The cutoff argument of lemma 5.27.40 shows that, under convergence in local capacity, every limit measure dominates the Monge–Ampère measure of the background; this gives a complete classification of the cluster sets for bounded backgrounds approximated from below. Convergence in local capacity is a stronger requirement than the $L^1$ convergence in Qin's general classification of reachable sets, whose argument for reaching the zero measure needs additional hypotheses on maximal approximation and on the domain; that argument is not used here.

Let $\phi _1,\ldots ,\phi _ r$ be plurisubharmonic weights with exponents $p_1,\ldots ,p_ r>1$, as in theorem 5.37.15. The division estimate with two summands, lemma 5.37.10, is the case of two weights in Takakura's [v1, Theorem 1.3, pp. 2 and 5–6, TakDivision26]. Since the relevant kernel is a line, the proof can use the Hessian formula for a scalar function instead of the general curvature theorem for subbundles. The constant in the a priori inequality (5.37.13) follows from the twisted Bochner identity in Demailly's notes [Section 13.A, pp. 123–124, DemAM11] by a weighted Cauchy inequality. Proposition 13.4 there states the weaker constant $2$; keeping the full factor $\eta +\lambda $ gives the constant $1$ used here. For a single weight, proposition 5.37.14 is the case $r=1$ of [Theorem 1.2, pp. 1–2 and 6–7, TakDivision26]. Applying it successively gives the product constant of theorem 5.37.15, with no condition on $\sum _ i1/p_ i$. The coordinate example in its proof extends [Example 3.2, p. 7, TakDivision26] and shows that this constant is optimal when $r\leq n$. For $2\leq r\leq n$ the product is strictly smaller than $1-r^{-1}\sum _ i1/p_ i$, the constant stated in Takakura's theorem. For $r>n$ the product need not improve Takakura's dimension-dependent estimate, and by itself it does not determine the optimal constant.

In dimension one, theorem 5.37.22 gives the optimal constant for every number $r$ of weights, including the range $\sum _ i1/p_ i\geq 1$ in which it vanishes. When $\sum _ i1/p_ i<1$, it equals the dimension-one constant of [Theorem 1.2, pp. 1–2, TakDivision26], and a common logarithmic pole shows that it is sharp. The local argument in lemma 5.37.18 uses the logarithmic fundamental solution and the characterization of positive distributions in [Chapter I, Sections 4.A–4.C, pp. 30–36, DemCADG]; in our normalization, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=\delta _0$. The global lifting in lemma 5.37.20 is the locally free planar case of vanishing for coherent sheaves. It is proved here with the vector-valued $L^2$ estimate for complete metrics in [Theorem 5.1 and its proof, pp. 33–34, DemAM11], whose Bochner identity is [Section 4.C, p. 30, DemAM11]. We do not determine the optimal constant when $n\geq 2$ and $r>n$.

25.3 Nonlinear products, capacity, and mass

25.3 Mass and energyE66D40EC5904

On a nonclosed background, the variation of the Monge–Ampère mass and the failure of the usual energy to have a primitive are related manifestations of torsion. Chiose's polarization argument [Theorems 1–2, Chiose16] gives the characterization of mass invariance in theorem 11.1.7. Yi Li constructed energies corrected by torsion terms [Equation (1.18) and Theorem 1.2, YiLi10]. The correction changes the one-form being integrated, in agreement with theorem 11.2.4, which shows, for $n\geq 2$, that the uncorrected one-form has no primitive unless $\omega $ is closed; proposition 11.2.10 computes the difference by a first variation.

Cutoffs of diffuse poles separate this variation of the background from a fixed loss of mass at the singularity. Let $n\geq 2$, and let $H$, $C$ and $M$ be the cutoff, the curvature constant and the residual mass of proposition 18.26.19; fix $0<t<1/C$ and put $A=\int _ X\omega ^ n$. The mass of $tH$ is a polynomial in $t$ whose finite torsion coefficients come from Stokes calculations for compactly supported bounded products. By proposition 18.26.21, every representative that is ordinarily bounded-equivalent to $tH$ loses the same top residual mass $Mt^ n$, although its lower-degree coefficients can vary. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ q)=0$ for $1\leq q<n$, invariance of the mass under bounded changes and invariance of the residual give the mass $A-Mt^ n$ throughout the class (corollary 18.26.20); this applies to every compact complex surface with a Gauduchon form. On a surface, corollary 18.26.22 shows that the mass is constant on the class if and only if $\omega $ is Gauduchon, since admissible smooth bounded perturbations detect any failure of the Gauduchon condition.

The failure of the bounded mass property on a Hopf threefold is the counterexample of Xia and Zhang [Theorem 1.1, XZ26]. There a Gauduchon background converts vertical Dirichlet energy into Monge–Ampère mass, a mechanism developed in section 23.1. Combined with theorem 13.14.18, it produces infinite extended mass with trivial multiplier ideals at every positive weight, and the results on integrability and convergence of coefficients in subsection 13.14.20 describe the linear current carried by this construction. Xia and Zhang use the operator $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $ [Section 1, XZ26]; dividing their background forms by $2\pi $ and leaving their potentials unchanged preserves positivity and changes the coefficient of the mass identity.

The local matrix, heat potential, Gaussian gradient estimate and completed square used in subsection 23.1.41 are those of Xia and Zhang [v1, Lemma 2.2, pp. 4–5; Lemmas 3.1–3.3, pp. 6–9; equation (4.2), p. 10, XZ26]. The faster initial time in theorem 23.1.52 changes the radial length and the integrated defect, so its positive correction is proved at that scale. The positive fiber flux and depth estimate give the square-root upper bound for all potentials in the declared unitary invariant class. The lower-density regions then give a single infinite weighted measure and concentration on a pole divisor at the critical weight; they also impose necessary conditions without the symmetry assumption. The unrestricted optimal sufficient rate remains open.

The passage from smooth to bounded and unbounded invariant potentials uses the classical bounded product and capacity theory developed in section 5.27, section 5.29. The local product construction and decreasing continuity are Bedford and Taylor's [Theorem 2.1, pp. 4–7; Theorem 2.4, pp. 7–9; Corollary 2.8, p. 10, BT82]; their quasi-continuity and zero-capacity results are [Theorem 3.5, p. 14; Theorems 6.9–6.10, pp. 25–26, BT82]. They use $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=2\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $, which is $4\pi $ times our operator and changes capacities only by a fixed factor. The local $L^1$ compactness underlying theorem 5.25.2 is also described in [Chapter I, Proposition 4.21, pp. 36–37; Proposition 5.9, p. 40, DemCADG]. In the present argument, group convolution and canonical truncation give the original Hermitian capacity convergence, including the boundary mass at a truncation level.

The extension in theorem 23.1.35 keeps the same threefold heat family. Its proof first bounds the actual mass on the negative radial half-line by exact integration over the elliptic fiber, then uses lemma 23.1.33 to compare the angularly integrated densities in different dimensions. The additional angular factor has a fixed positive lower bound on the half-line carrying the divergent mass. Corollary 23.1.36 transfers this failure to every Hermitian metric on the same scalar Hopf manifold.

The failure of positive lower mass is a different phenomenon; it occurs on the elliptic threefold of section 12.19. Sufficient conditions for a positive lower bound come instead from the sign of the torsion: (12.16.4) is the three-dimensional case of a formula of Angella, Guedj and Lu [Theorem 3.2, AGL23], who call the condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$ plurinegativity.

The principal elliptic bundles of subsection 24.4.7 are special cases of the torus bundles of Goldstein and Prokushkin [Section 2, GP04]. The metric calculation on these bundles gives an upper bound for the mass, but it does not decide whether the lower mass vanishes. The radial calculation of proposition 24.4.13 bounds the root volume of the specified affine test family at fixed degree; the lower mass over all potentials remains open.

The completion energy of subsection 11.2.14 is the Dinew–Popovici functional. Hanwen Liu defines it and computes its variations in [v1, Section 2.1, pp. 3–5, LiuCritical26], and proves the identity relating energy and volume along potential variations, together with the indefiniteness of the Hessian, in [Theorems 5.1–5.2, pp. 16–19, LiuCritical26]. Liu assumes that the ambient manifold is Kähler. The proofs in the book use only the finite-dimensional space of closed holomorphic completions and Stokes' theorem, so these statements about potential variations hold on every compact Hermitian symplectic fourfold. Liu's calculation of criticality for products [Lemma 2.3 and Theorem 2.4, pp. 7–9, LiuCritical26] gives the mechanism of example 11.2.23, where an explicit Fourier form on the square torus replaces the general existence argument on surfaces. Neither the general existence criterion of that paper in terms of the canonical bundle nor its convergence theorem for the global torsion flow is used here. Liu's convention is $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm i(\bar\partial -\partial )$; rewritten with the book's $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, the formulas of that paper for potential variations give (11.2.20) with the coefficients shown there. Combined with Chiose's criterion, the energy identity gives the equivalence between flatness of the energy and invariance of the mass in corollary 11.2.21. The calculation with one nonclosed factor in example 11.2.24 shows that this flatness along potentials implies neither criticality in the full Aeppli class nor the existence of a primitive for the Monge–Ampère one-form.

25.3 Nonlinear products, capacity, and mass

25.3 Bounded products and extended measuresE66D40EC5904

The Bedford–Taylor product of bounded potentials is local even when the background is not closed: expanding against smooth local corrections, as Kołodziej and Nguyen [Section 1, KN15] and Boucksom, Guedj and Lu [Section 2.1, BGL25] do, gives proposition 5.28.2. Restricting the products of the truncations to the sets where the potential exceeds the truncation level then defines the extended measure of theorem 13.14.3, by the mechanism of [Proposition 2.1, BGL25]. Finiteness becomes decisive when these restrictions are removed in the category of currents, and [Theorem 2.2, BGL25] uses a uniform bound on the variation for this purpose. An infinite extended positive measure is still given by the local construction, but it is not a global current of order zero.

The independence of the bounded mass property from the metric, and the reduction to smooth potentials, in proposition 13.14.15 recover the comparison made after [Definition 1.16, BGL25]; decreasing regularization with exact curvature bounds gives the passage from smooth to bounded potentials. The Gauduchon trace bound and the cancellation of the exact top-degree wedge product used in proposition 13.15.2 also appear in Guedj and Lu's [Proposition 3.3(i), (vi), GL22], and the estimate in terms of the range of the potential keeps their polynomial dependence on the oscillation.

The local mixed Monge–Ampère inequality, theorem 5.27.5, is Dinew's [Theorem 1.2, Dinew09], for locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions whose Monge–Ampère measures dominate nonnegative measurable densities with respect to Lebesgue measure. Its extension to smooth backgrounds is proved in section 5.28 and used in subsection 15.18.2. Freezing the coefficients of the two smooth backgrounds gives lemma 5.28.7 and the trace inequalities (15.14.3) and lemma 13.14.12, the latter keeping the mass of the linear trace on the pole set. The same argument also recovers the inequality for smooth volume forms used by Nguyen [Lemma 1.9, Nguyen16].

25.4 Positivity, Hermitian geometry, and volume

25.4 Gauduchon metrics and positivityF9B38BEB0BCF

Gauduchon metrics replace the cohomological conservation of mass by a linear trace identity. In the form recalled by Tosatti and Weinkove immediately before [Lemma 2.3, TW10], Gauduchon's conformal theorem starts, in dimension $n\geq 2$, from a Hermitian form $\eta $ and constructs a smooth real function $f$ such that $\gamma =\mathrm e^ f\eta $ is Gauduchon; the multiplier in theorem 11.4.2 is then $\rho =\mathrm e^{(n-1)f}$. The resulting trace comparison, corollary 11.5.3, also underlies the first mixed-volume bounds of Guedj and Lu [Proposition 3.3, GL22].

For lemma 11.24.1, the constant-coefficient estimate is the order-zero multiplier theorem in Taylor [Chapter 13, Theorem 5.1 and its proof, pp. 16–21, Taylor13]; compactness is [Chapter 13, (6.9), p. 24, Taylor13]. Freezing the continuous coefficients gives the Sobolev estimate, and the proof writes out the classical Alexandrov–Bakelman–Pucci contact-set bound and tangent-ball maximum principle before applying the method of continuity and compact-perturbation index theory. It does not differentiate the coefficients.

The trace identity has a dual form: positivity can be tested against Gauduchon metrics. For an arbitrary smooth background, the generalized Lamari criterion theorem 11.6.1 is stated by Boucksom, Guedj and Lu [Lemma 1.15, BGL25]; its proof combines a separation argument with a right inverse of a scalar elliptic operator. In theorem 11.8.1, Lamari duality combines with normalized compactness and Siu analyticity to turn bounded transverse test pairings into a global hypersurface. The regularized logarithmic potentials in proposition 11.8.2 give the converse bound when a Cartier divisor agrees with the cutoff hypersurface throughout its chart. The same linear control gives the bound (11.5.6) for the normalization constant, which is used in the weak existence arguments of [Section 4, BGL25].

The deformation obstruction for convex norms in theorem 11.9.4 is due to Liu and Wan [v1, Theorem 3.2 and Sections 3.1–3.3, pp. 9–13, LiuWanKobayashi26], and the normalization of line metrics in lemma 11.9.1 is their Lemma 3.1, p. 8. The proof combines derivative estimates along the line axes with an average of the horizontal curvature and the formal adjoint on a fixed sphere bundle. The resulting $C^4$ neighborhood is uniform over all smooth complex norms, and the positive Gauduchon test forms may differ from one line summand to another.

The regularization of homogeneous functions in theorem 11.10.4 is the case of a compact base of a lemma of Kuang-Ru Wu [v1, Section 2.3, Lemma 13, pp. 10–13, WuFinslerIII23]. Its gluing step uses the closure under maxima, the stability under smooth perturbations and the semilocal approximation of Greene and Wu [Definitions 1.1, 1.3–1.4, pp. 48–49; Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.1, pp. 80–81, GreeneWu79], while the local positivity properties are proved directly from a holomorphic shear formula. The replacement in proposition 11.10.5 assumes that a strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function is given, and corollary 11.10.6 keeps the hypothesis of local strong convexity in the fibers.

The local example example 11.10.1 adapts the quadratic maximum of Fukuoka and Setti [v1, Example 3.18, p. 20, FukuokaSettiStrongConvex26] to a complex rank-two bundle over a disk. A geometric series of squared holomorphic moduli gives its total-space plurisubharmonicity. Its fiberwise quadratic margin tends to zero at nearby base points, showing why local strong convexity in theorem 11.10.4 requires a common margin on a total-space neighborhood. The example concerns this distinction between hypotheses; the general real-Finsler smoothing and connection-convergence theorems of that paper are not used.

The existence result of Liu and Wan [v1, Theorem 2.1, p. 7, LiuWanKobayashi26] that is needed here is proved directly by the tautological construction of lemma 11.11.1, proposition 11.11.2: a metric with positive curvature on the dual of the tautological line bundle gives a homogeneous squared norm that is strictly plurisubharmonic off the zero section. When the dual vector bundle is ample, such a line metric is a root of the Fubini–Study metric pulled back by a very ample embedding. The result is the strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function used in their regularization [v1, Lemma 3.4, pp. 13–14, LiuWanKobayashi26], and it gives corollary 11.11.3.

The construction of polar norms in 11.12 gives a proof of Liu and Wan's [v1, Proposition 3.5, pp. 14–16, LiuWanKobayashi26]. A Schur complement and a holomorphic correction of the second jet give local pluriharmonic supporting functions for the logarithm of the polar square. A uniform upper bound for the real Hessian of the primal squared metric gives strong convexity of the dual through its exact Legendre expression; neither real convexity of the primal metric nor uniqueness of a maximizer is assumed. The tautological construction for an ample dual and the homogeneous regularization then give the smooth replacement and the curvature obstruction of corollary 11.12.7, under the hypotheses stated there.

On Hirzebruch surfaces, the ample comparison quotient and the two prioritary points of proposition 11.13.2, lemma 11.13.3 are Liu and Wan's [v1, Proposition 4.2 and Lemma 4.3, pp. 17–20, LiuWanKobayashi26]. The facts about Hirzebruch surfaces that they need are proved directly in lemma 11.13.1, from sections along the ruling and a very ample embedding. The positive Gauduchon tests for the individual dual line bundles in proposition 11.13.4 are the divisor calculation in their proof of Theorem 1.1, p. 23. These constructions give the ample point and the test forms used in theorem 11.15.5, corollary 11.15.6.

The stability of extensions in proposition 11.14.1 is Liu and Wan's [v1, Proposition 4.4, pp. 20–21, LiuWanKobayashi26], including the equality case on $\mathbb F_0$. The proof of proposition 11.14.2 uses the exact sequences of $\operatorname {Hom}$ groups and applies to every extension, while restriction to a fiber of the ruling shows that none of them is ample. The explicit family of Dolbeault operators in proposition 11.14.3 converges to the split operator in every finite $C^ m$ norm. These stable, nonample approximations give the stable point used in the deformation argument of theorem 11.15.5.

The approximation theorem theorem 11.15.5 is Liu and Wan's [v1, Theorem 4.1, p. 17; proof, p. 22, LiuWanKobayashi26]. Its input on the stack of prioritary sheaves is Walter's [v1, Proposition 2, p. 2, WalterPrioritary93], which applies to all prioritary torsion-free sheaves of fixed rank at least two with fixed numerical Chern classes, without any semistability assumption. The required openness statements are proved directly by the family arguments in lemma 11.15.1, lemma 11.15.2, lemma 11.15.3; on a Hirzebruch surface, slope stability reduces to finitely many classes of line bundles. Parallel transport and compactness, in lemma 11.15.4, give convergence on the fixed smooth bundle and on its dual in every finite $C^ m$ norm. Combining this approximation with the Gauduchon-degree obstruction and the polar construction above gives corollary 11.15.6, which is Liu and Wan's [v1, Theorem 1.1, p. 2; proof, p. 23, LiuWanKobayashi26].

The fixed Stein hypersurface of theorem 11.16.3, corollary 11.16.4 corresponds to Liu and Wan's [v1, Proposition 5.1, pp. 24–27, LiuWanKobayashi26] for explicit algebraic bundles. A positive horizontal direction and the vertical critical hyperplane give the test on the Levi index, and a holomorphic quadratic jet makes the real Hessian nondegenerate without changing the Levi form. Separability of the relevant metric space gives countably many robust local tests, which lemma 11.16.1, lemma 11.16.2 place on a single global graph by Runge and Oka–Weil approximation. The graph is chosen before the metric, whereas the critical point that detects the failure may depend on the metric.

The dual norm of a concave neighborhood, theorem 11.17.2, is Liu and Wan's [v1, Lemma 5.2, pp. 27–32, LiuWanKobayashi26]. After a correction by a pure jet, a negative tangent plane of the boundary gives a supporting holomorphic section. Balls of uniform size tangent to the boundary from inside then express the squared dual norm as a supremum of functions with a common margin of strong real convexity, and ampleness together with homogeneous regularization gives a smooth replacement. Let $E$ be an ample bundle of rank $r$, and write $U_ E=\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X\oplus E)\setminus \mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X)$ for the complement of the zero section in its projective completion. The argument at high levels of an exhaustion in corollary 11.17.4, which shows that $U_ E$ is not $r$-convex when $E^*$ admits no smooth complex norm with plurisubharmonic square, is their [v1, Corollary 5.3, p. 32, LiuWanKobayashi26]. Combined with the norm obstruction and the stable ample approximation, it gives corollary 11.17.5.

The case of positive mean curvature in theorem 11.18.2, corollary 11.18.4 is Liu and Wan's [v1, Proposition 5.4, pp. 32–33, LiuWanKobayashi26]. The calculation with the reciprocal of the norm gives the more general count, in which $s$ positive horizontal directions of the curvature give $(n+r-s)$-convexity of $U_ E$ for a bundle $E$ of rank $r$. For stable bundles of positive degree, the application uses the existence of Hermitian–Einstein metrics, proved by Uhlenbeck and Yau [UhlenbeckYau86] in the Kähler case and extended to Gauduchon metrics by Li and Yau [LiYau87]. The degree of definition 11.18.3 pairs the Bott–Chern first Chern class with the Gauduchon form; with the unscaled curvature $F_ h$ of a Hermitian metric $h$, the integrated trace carries the factor $2\pi n$. The resulting least convexity index three in corollary 11.18.5 is [v1, Corollary 5.5, p. 33, LiuWanKobayashi26]; the lower bound uses the dual-norm obstruction above.

The negative-bundle weight in proposition 11.19.1 is the construction of Kusakabe and Matsumura [v1, Lemma 3.2(a,b,d), pp. 20–21, KusakabeMatsumuraOka26]. The complete metric of corollary 11.19.3 uses the two exhaustion barriers in the first paragraph of their proof of [v1, Lemma 3.3, p. 21, KusakabeMatsumuraOka26]. Their jet-vanishing condition [v1, Lemma 3.4, p. 21, KusakabeMatsumuraOka26] follows here from the smooth-center multiplier-ideal formula, which gives the exact ideal and the sharp threshold for every real weight in corollary 11.19.2. In their argument the logarithmic weight supports weighted $\bar\partial $ estimates and the gluing of local sprays; here its direct Levi calculation relates negative bundle curvature to the singularity along the zero section.

Suppose that, for a holomorphic bundle $F$ of rank $r$, the complement $F^\times $ of the zero section carries a smooth positive plurisubharmonic function that is homogeneous of degree two. Taking maxima over the level spheres, proposition 11.21.1 then shows that the least convexity index of $U_ F$ is $n+r$: a negative radial derivative makes the Levi form restricted to the level set nonpositive on a complex hyperplane. Unitary-flat metrics give corollary 11.21.3. For the line bundles $E_ a$ on a Hopf manifold in example 11.21.4, restriction to an elliptic fiber and positive curvature give the least index two when $|a|<1$, whereas a homogeneous plurisubharmonic metric gives the least index $n+1$ when $|a|\geq 1$; the Gauduchon degree distinguishes the three signs, although the de Rham first Chern class vanishes. A metric with Griffiths-nonpositive curvature gives the same homogeneous function in corollary 11.21.2. For split bundles on Hopf manifolds, proposition 11.21.5 combines the weighted curvature with the exact loss of dimension under restriction to closed submanifolds in lemma 11.17.3. It gives the least indices $r+1$ and $n+r$ in the two pure regimes; in the mixed regime, only separate upper and lower bounds are obtained.

For external tensor products, theorem 11.20.2 applies the same exhaustion with one positive curvature direction from each factor. The positive mean curvatures lifted from the factors control every vector of the tensor product, including the indecomposable ones, and give corollary 11.20.3. For the tangent bundle of a surface with a nonflat Ricci-flat Kähler metric, corollary 11.27.5 combines the exhaustion instead with the directional positivity of theorem 11.27.4: this tangent bundle admits no metric whose mean curvature is positive definite, but its RC-positive metric still gives the required exhaustion.

For the logarithmic parabolic Monge–Ampère flow on Kähler manifolds, the calculation of $L^ p$ norms of the volume ratio is Jiyuan Han's [v1, Lemma 3.2, pp. 13–14, HanParabolic26]. The chain rule and Stokes computation in proposition 11.23.8 keep the additional term coming from the derivative of the Hermitian background. When the forms along the flow remain Gauduchon, convex entropies decrease (corollary 11.23.11), and varying the target probability measure gives the exact criterion at the initial time in proposition 11.23.12. These statements apply on any interval on which a smooth solution exists. Han's uniform estimates for degenerating families of Calabi–Yau manifolds, and the Green-function estimates on which they depend, are not part of this calculation.

The calculation of the total variation in proposition 11.23.16 is a direct variation of determinants on a flat torus, whose coefficient is given by the two Haar averages of lemma 11.23.14. Corollary 11.23.17 compares this growth of the distance between two solutions with the initial derivatives of the individual entropies.

The support lemma for currents carried by a smooth hypersurface, lemma 11.22.1, is the local statement used by Dinh and Sibony in [proof of Theorem 4.1, pp. 965–966, DinhSibonyRegularization04], where it is attributed to Bassanelli. The proof given here tests against a quadratic function of the normal coordinate and polarizes horizontal forms; it applies whenever $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ has order zero, $R$ being the positive current supported on the hypersurface. The estimate for pullbacks in lemma 11.22.2 follows directly from the classical $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-lemma for currents on compact Kähler manifolds, applied to a fixed closed pushforward; the current that is paired with the distributional primitive is smooth.

The smoothing of positive pluriharmonic forms with continuous coefficients in lemma 11.22.3 uses the heat equation of the Hodge Laplacian, the Kähler identities and a positive correction tending to zero. For continuous potentials and closed backgrounds on a compact Kähler manifold, Dinh and Sibony construct the product of the curvature current with a positive pluriharmonic current through an energy [Theorem 5.1, Proposition 5.2 and identity (12), pp. 967–969, DinhSibonyRegularization04]. The proofs of lemma 11.31.10, theorem 11.31.11 integrate by parts against the current of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$ itself, so that no auxiliary power of a Kähler form is needed. They give a positive measure as product, depending jointly continuously on the factors, on any compact Hermitian manifold, for every smooth real background and continuous potential.

The descent of horizontal currents in lemma 11.22.4 follows directly from the positivity of the coefficient matrix together with the Liouville theorem for harmonic functions on the complex line, or the maximum principle on a compact connected curve. It therefore applies both to bundles with fiber $\mathbb C$ and to bundles of compact curves. On the elliptic threefold, the exact vertical trace form gives lemma 10.19.1 for positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed currents, and its closed case gives the calculation of the Bott–Chern cone.

The mean-curvature criterion for RC-positivity and the conformal construction in lemma 11.26.2, theorem 11.26.3 correspond to Chou and Wu's [v1, Definition 5 and Lemmas 7–8, pp. 5–6, ChouWuRC26]. The scalar equation in the construction is the Gauduchon compatibility condition of proposition 11.23.2, and taking the curvature margin over a closed ball makes it uniform in both the base point and the unit fiber vector. Example 11.26.6 shows directly that the order of these two quantifiers matters, and proposition 11.26.7 gives a global obstruction to interchanging them when the determinant bundle admits a flat Hermitian metric.

The RC-positive tangent metrics on Ricci-flat surfaces in theorem 11.27.4 are Chou and Wu's [v1, Theorem 1 and Lemmas 9–15, pp. 7–12, ChouWuRC26]. The pointwise criterion is the invertibility of the anti-self-dual curvature operator. The identities behind (11.27.3) are Derdziński's [equations (33)–(35), p. 414, Derdzinski83], with the nonnegative Laplacian on functions used there replaced by $\operatorname {div}\nabla $ and with the same norm on endomorphisms; summing the three equations for the eigenvalues gives the coefficient $36$. The commuting curvature factors in [Lemma 2, p. 412, Derdzinski83] also show directly that a nonzero parallel operator with three distinct eigenvalues cannot occur here. This gives the required nonempty open set and a conformal tangent metric whose associated form is not closed.

The symmetrized sectional-curvature average and the integrated trace identity in lemma 11.28.2, proposition 11.28.3 are Xueyuan Wan's [v1, Lemma 2.1 and Proposition 3.3 with Lemmas 3.1–3.2, pp. 5–8, WanHermitianSectional26]. The average is proved here by complex Gaussian moments, and the connection calculation retains the exact term until Stokes' theorem removes it. The auxiliary metric $g$ is Kähler, while the tangent metric $h$ can be nonclosed. Their identity gives corollary 11.28.5 directly from the signs of its three terms. This use of the identity does not require the auxiliary Hessian equation or the canonical-bundle positivity argument of that paper. The torus and finite torus-cover statements of proposition 11.28.7, corollary 11.28.8 follow from this identity and periodic integration by parts: the symmetric connection difference vanishes, forcing the Hermitian coefficients to be constant. In dimension one, the same conclusion is the maximum principle for the logarithm of the metric coefficient.

The first-jet characterization of Griffiths positivity on projective manifolds, theorem 11.29.9, is due to Du and Xie [v1, Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 2.1, pp. 1–4, DuXieFirstJet26]; the identity in normal frames is written in the curvature convention used above. The density with two derivatives that the argument requires is proved directly in lemma 11.29.6, lemma 11.29.7, through normalized projective coordinates and Bernstein polynomials. The immersion test without twist, corollary 11.29.10, is the calculation in [v1, Section 3.1, pp. 4–5, DuXieFirstJet26]. The positive measure in the dual alternative lives on the sphere bundle of the dual bundle, so the condition that it annihilates all metrics is different from Gauduchon duality on the base.

The double cover in section 11.30, branched over $2q$ points, gives an explicit model with a computable space of sections in which a strictly positive line bundle fails the test without twist. The decomposition of sections into even and odd parts and the projective embedding are proved explicitly. A root of a very ample Fubini–Study metric gives a separately defined weighted family of tests, and proposition 11.30.3 identifies its first successful level $j=q-1$, together with obstructions by one or two atoms at the lower levels. The original criterion with a fixed very ample twist $m$ follows the subsequence $j=qm$, so this calculation does not determine its first successful twist. The obstructions at a single level should also be distinguished from an adjoint measure annihilating every smooth metric.

25.4 Positivity, Hermitian geometry, and volume

25.4 Volumes under mass boundsF9B38BEB0BCF

For a nonclosed background, the mass of a single potential does not determine the masses in its singularity type. The lower and upper volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ of definition 16.28.58, the infimum and the supremum of the mass over the ordinary singularity type of $u$, record the information that a single mass loses. Under bounded mass, comparison of these volumes controls envelopes and defines a topology on models of positive lower volume. On curves, polar curvature describes the boundary where the lower volume vanishes.

25.4 Positivity, Hermitian geometry, and volume

25.4 Singularity volumes and relative classesF9B38BEB0BCF

The volumes used in section 13.17 are those of Boucksom, Guedj and Lu [Definition 3.1, BGL25], expressed in terms of potentials. For closed backgrounds the two volumes coincide, because the non-pluripolar mass is invariant under bounded changes of the potential, as recalled in [Example 3.2, BGL25]. In the big case, the monotonicity theorem theorem 13.17.1 is [Proposition 3.7, BGL25], and the argument for lower volumes in proposition 13.17.2 is Li's [Proposition 2.5, XL26].

The order test in 13.24.8 uses the projective valuative characterization of Darvas and Xia [Theorem 2.13 and Proposition 2.30, DX22] in a common closed Kähler background. Their Lelong convention differs from the divisor coefficient used here by a factor of two, which leaves equality of order profiles unchanged. The countable divisorial domination and envelope arguments are those of lemma 5.38.5, corollary 18.4.9; they identify the whole ordinary type before its mass is computed. The upper bound for the closed top mass uses Witt Nyström's monotonicity theorem [WN19], while the lower bound follows directly from local bounded truncations. Expansion with smooth corrections, as in [Section 2.1, BGL25], then gives the nonclosed mass throughout this type. This computation applies to the prescribed summable hyperplane profile with positive smooth residual; it does not assert mass invariance for arbitrary unbounded types in a pluriclosed background.

The relative full-mass class of definition 13.18.4 is [Definition 3.2, XL26]. The stretching criterion lemma 13.18.1 is [Lemma 3.1, XL26]; the proof given here keeps track of the deficit of upper volumes and chooses a representative whose mass is close to its upper volume. The case of zero deficit gives theorem 13.18.5, and a uniform bound for Lelong numbers turns the convex comparisons into the estimate of proposition 13.18.3.

The domination principle theorem 13.19.1 is [Proposition 3.2, XL26]; its proof uses that the reference has positive lower volume, but not that it is an envelope fixed point. The estimate for relative obstacles, lemma 13.19.4, is [Proposition 3.3, XL26]. Together they give the identity for upper volumes in [Lemma 3.2, XL26] and the identity for lower volumes in [Corollary 3.3, XL26], both stated in theorem 13.19.5. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the proof first shows that the increasing limit of the obstacle envelopes has the ordinary singularity type of $P_\theta [u]$, so that domination can be applied before the equality of volumes is established. The resulting characterization of full mass gives the volume criterion in proposition 13.24.2.

When the pole set is compact of Hausdorff dimension zero and the lower volume is positive, theorem 13.19.6 shows that ordinary projection preserves the whole residual measure. Bounded mass gives uniform bounds for the traces of all local closed powers of the ordinary rooftop envelopes. Away from the pole set, convergence in capacity of bounded functions identifies the limits, and the Hausdorff estimate removes all mass of the lower-degree coefficients on the pole set; hence the lower-degree global pairings preserve the full total mass. Since the rooftop envelopes all have the same residual measure, positivity together with the local order of residuals forces the model to have this residual as well. The argument also identifies the weak limit of the full Monge–Ampère measures of these rooftop envelopes. The sources of the local inputs are given in section 25.2.

The construction of small stretches, lemma 13.20.1, is [Proposition 3.1, XL26], and its bound for mixed masses gives an explicit uniform scale of stretching. The additive estimate for lower volumes in proposition 13.20.6 is the case of smooth perturbations of [Proposition 3.3(ii), BGL25], with the mixed bound of [Lemma 2.4, BGL25] written in terms of potentials. The strict barrier gives the multiplicative comparison at positive lower volume, as in [Proposition 3.5(ii), Step 1, XL26]. Consequently, corollary 13.21.4 gives continuity of the lower volume of every fixed potential as the background varies, while continuity of the upper volume and of the ordinary envelope still requires positive lower volume.

The continuity along increasing sequences, theorem 13.21.1, is [Proposition 3.5(i), XL26]: contact identifies the limit of the envelopes and its upper volume, and the deficit estimate then shows that the approximating lower volumes are positive. The continuity along decreasing sequences of models, theorem 13.21.2, is [Proposition 3.5(ii), XL26], including its conclusion when the lower volume of the limit vanishes. The uniform small stretch shows that a positive lower bound along the models forces their limit to have positive lower volume, and strict corrections and tail envelopes reduce the variation of the background to the argument for a fixed background. Li states the result for perturbations $\theta +\varepsilon _ j\omega $ with $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, whereas the proof here treats arbitrary smooth backgrounds that decrease uniformly in the order of forms. The criterion for positive lower volume, proposition 13.21.3, is [Proposition 3.5(iii), XL26]. The deficit bound gives uniform convergence of Lelong numbers on each fixed compact model, and the envelopes of the restricted analytic approximants give the exact traces of corollary 13.21.5.

For semipositive backgrounds, proposition 13.20.4 is the forward direction of [Proposition 2.11, ALS26], deduced here from the strict barrier. This direction requires neither the identity for ordinary envelopes nor positivity of the lower mass $v_-(\theta )$ of definition 13.14.14; that assumption is used for the converse. Applied to an envelope fixed point, the proposition compares Li's condition (13.20.5) with the condition (16.28.67) of Alehyane, Lu and Salouf.

25.4 Positivity, Hermitian geometry, and volume

25.4 Model topology and analytic approximationF9B38BEB0BCF

The comparison function $d_\theta $ of definition 13.22.1, defined through the upper volumes of two potentials and of their maximum, is introduced in [Section 4.2, XL26]. That it separates models follows from the characterization by envelopes. The normalized stretching argument of [Lemma 4.2, XL26] gives the quantitative $L^1$ bound in proposition 13.22.4, and the three-point estimate (13.22.6) passes convergence from a subsequence to the whole Cauchy sequence. The construction by maxima of tails in theorem 13.22.7 follows [Theorem 4.3, XL26], with a fixed $\delta >0$ and the non-strict lower bound $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\geq \delta $. The strict bound $>\delta $ used in version 1 of Li's preprint is not preserved under limits of Cauchy sequences, as example 13.22.8 shows. Li explicitly allows $d_\theta $ to violate the triangle inequality, and example 13.27.1 gives an example of such a failure with intersecting divisors.

The criterion for finite rooftop envelopes, lemma 13.23.1, is [Lemma 4.1, XL26]: after choosing representatives whose masses are close to their upper volumes, a collapse would contradict the lower volume of the common upper bound. Li's argument with softened stretches [Proposition 4.4, XL26] gives proposition 13.23.2; only the limiting potential needs positive lower volume, and the same comparison gives convergence of the lower volumes of the rooftop envelopes. The two stretching scales in [Theorem 4.4, XL26] produce the monotone bounds of theorem 13.23.3. Since finite rooftop envelopes are again normalized models, continuity along decreasing models passes their volume bounds to the infinite tails; monotone convergence in capacity then applies, and the subsequence criterion gives convergence of the original sequence.

The results on analytic approximation in section 13.24 combine this continuity of volumes with the limit of the dyadic multiplier-ideal envelopes. Mixing with a strict analytic potential, with rational coefficients, removes the curvature error in any smooth big background, and two comparisons of backgrounds then give the exact excess of upper volume in (13.24.4). Conversely, stretching and concavity of the multiplier-ideal envelope show that its fixed points are closed under the upper-volume comparison at positive lower volume. This proves the analytic criterion theorem 13.24.5 and the Cauchy completeness inherited there. The boundary where the lower volume vanishes in higher dimension, and positivity criteria in terms of ideals, are the separate questions of 13.24.11.

The comparisons of backgrounds in section 13.25 follow from the same arguments with volumes and envelopes. Transport by a smooth gauge preserves the competitor currents, and ordinary projection corrects the zero obstacle; the explicit scale of small stretches makes the strict barrier uniform on sets of models whose lower volumes are bounded below by a positive constant. This yields (13.25.4) and extends the analytic criterion to positive background errors that tend to zero. These statements concern singularity volumes and canonical models; they neither identify the mass of the unregularized envelope with a gauge invariant nor assert convergence of arbitrary representatives.

The two-sided transport in section 13.26 mixes the original model with a strict analytic potential. A common upper background bounds both this transport and the maximum of two transported models, and the resulting volume bounds give uniform comparison, convergence of the transported reference, and equivalence of the limiting comparisons obtained with different strict corrections. The estimate for nearby backgrounds and the three-point modulus then reduce the analytic criterion of that section to theorem 13.25.5.

The complete metric in section 13.27 is obtained by the standard construction with finite dyadic chains, carried out directly from the three-point modulus. Stretching first gives continuity of the lower volume, and the reciprocal of the lower volume controls the boundary where it vanishes; the statement about the analytic completion then follows from the approximation criterion above. This metric induces the topology of the upper-volume comparison; it does not turn the comparison function itself into a metric.

In dimension $n\geq 2$, polar curvature on all modifications still does not detect all ordinary models. The Cantor construction of example 13.28.14 gives the curve potentials of lemma 18.26.15; their maximum has vanishing first polar currents, but its truncations keep a positive top-degree mass $M$ near the common pole set. A rank bound for smooth maxima gives the construction in every dimension. By proposition 18.26.17, corollary 18.26.18, every compact Kähler manifold, with Kähler form $\omega $ and $A=\int _ X\omega ^ n$, carries a complete ordered interval of diffuse models $p_ t$ with volumes $A-Mt^ n$ and distances $M|s^ n-t^ n|$ between $p_ s$ and $p_ t$, and every choice of the first polar comparison collapses this interval. Hence the closure of the analytic models for the polar comparison contains models that are not ideal. The identities for invariant mass extend these formulas to the setting of corollary 18.26.20.

For an arbitrary Hermitian background with bounded mass and positive lower mass, the mass bounds for representatives give proposition 18.26.23. This applies to every Hermitian metric on a compact complex surface, by the existence of Gauduchon metrics, the independence of the bounded mass property from the metric (proposition 13.14.15) and corollary 12.19.15. Preservation of residuals and additivity of volumes then give corollary 18.26.24 for all parameters in the strict range. The upper volume along this interval is strictly decreasing and Lipschitz, although in general the length of the interval is not given by the power formula valid for closed backgrounds, and all first polar coordinates still vanish. In proposition 18.26.25, two cutoffs with disjoint supports have equal total residual masses and vanishing first polar data, yet their maximum is zero and their distance is positive; in backgrounds with invariant mass, both singularity volumes coincide as well. These scalar data therefore cannot recover the spatial distribution of the residual mass.

A direct calculation with maxima in lemma 18.26.16 identifies the full residual measure as the tensor product of the measures on the curve factors, multiplied by the product of the positive weights; for a smooth maximum the coefficient reduces to the volume of a simplex. In proposition 18.26.26, a common cutoff and a uniform curvature bound give a compact family of models indexed by a box of positive weights. Invariance under projection identifies the comparison distance in this family, up to a fixed scale, with the Lebesgue measure of the symmetric difference of coordinate rectangles. The subfamilies on which the product of the weights is constant are complete and have real dimension $n-1$, although their members have the same full residual measure on $X$, the same two singularity volumes, the same multiplier ideals and the same first polar currents. The construction takes place in a background with invariant mass and concerns the residual measure on $X$ itself; it does not identify the full residual products on every modification. The problem of describing the complete topology remains open.

25.4 Positivity, Hermitian geometry, and volume

25.4 Curves and zero-volume limitsF9B38BEB0BCF

The inverse maximum principle in the plane, lemma 5.27.14, is the two-dimensional case of the result stated by Brezis and Ponce [Theorem 3.1, BP04], who attribute it to Dupaigne and Ponce; the proof given here uses harmonic barriers on shrinking neighborhoods of a compact polar set. Applied to differences of potentials, it shows that the polar curvature measures are ordered as the potentials are, and subtracting a common Green potential gives the formula (5.27.16) for the maximum. Since these local facts are general, they are proved in section 5.21.

The classification of models on curves in section 13.28 combines this order of polar measures with the Green representation of subsection 20.3.9. Every prescribed polar measure gives an ordinary model equivalent to its Green potential, and the characterization of envelopes of positive mass, together with uniqueness of harmonic functions at zero mass, identifies every ordinary envelope with such a model. The formula for the maximum then turns the upper-volume comparison into the total variation of measures, and completeness, geodesics and the nearest ideal model follow from the corresponding operations on measures. The exact defect of analytic approximation is the nonatomic polar mass, which for the Cantor example is the full curvature mass.

For a finite map of curves, the fiber maximum in 5.43.15 follows from the local branched coordinates and the removable-singularity theorem for subharmonic functions. The weighted trace in 5.43.16 includes the local degrees at atoms; its agreement with current pullback follows from the Riesz representation on a disk and the Poincaré–Lelong formula. These elementary operations give the envelope identities of 18.24.1. Applying the curve classification gives the degree-scaled metric embedding and the averaging retraction of 18.24.2. The component factorization then gives the complete subspace of models descending to the original base in 18.24.3. The cubic example 18.24.4 distinguishes this averaging from the nearest ideal retraction.

The continuity statement for curves, theorem 13.28.8, uses the theorem on convergence in capacity at positive volume in the interior. At zero mass the polar curvature is the whole current, which gives convergence of the currents in total variation. The local estimate lemma 5.27.11, which follows from the Green representation on a disk, the mean-value estimate for harmonic functions and the weighted Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality, gives convergence in capacity at this boundary. Moving a pole distinguishes this topology from that of total variation, while the approximation by finitely many atoms in theorem 18.6.4 distinguishes weak convergence of the curvature currents from convergence in capacity.

The correspondences between backgrounds in section 13.29 follow from the same classification by polar measures, which smooth gauges extend to every smooth background of positive area on a curve. Changes of background with equal area preserve total variation, whereas rescaling the area gives homotheties compatible with extraction of atoms and hence with ideal projection. These correspondences are realized by a smooth gauge, obtained from the scalar Poisson equation, followed by ordinary projection. Comparing the new obstacle with its maximum and minimum gives a uniform bound, which yields continuity in $L^1$ and in capacity up to the boundary of zero mass. Rationality is needed only for the assertion that analytic singularities are preserved under rescaling of the area, because analytic singularities in this book have rational coefficients. At zero area, positivity and Stokes' theorem leave a single normalized potential. The general convergence statement theorem 5.29.23, proved in section 5.21, follows from compactness of normalized potentials, uniqueness of harmonic functions and the local estimate relating total variation and capacity. It also gives the collapse of the model representatives as the unscaled metric diameters tend to zero.

25.4 Positivity, Hermitian geometry, and volume

25.4 Gauduchon variational volumeF9B38BEB0BCF

The Gauduchon variational volume extracts a homogeneous concave quantity from an elliptic normalization problem. The method goes back to Collins's construction [Theorem 2.13, Collins21]; section 12.1 develops the adjoint formula and its dependence on the chosen probability measure.

For a Kähler class represented by a closed form $\theta $, this construction meets the Hessian geometry of the Kähler cone: the metric of section 12.4 is $1/n$ times the Hessian of $-\log \int _ X\theta ^ n$ used by Magnússon [Section 1, Magnusson12]. Completeness and boundary points of positive volume at finite distance are studied in [Proposition 4.4 and Lemma 4.5, Magnusson12]; section 12.6 gives the argument by homogeneity in the present normalization.

The cones of invariant nonclosed forms in subsection 12.6.4 are computed directly. Stokes' theorem on the compact quotient shows that invariant $(n-1,n-1)$-forms are closed, and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for matrices then determines the quotient and its normalized minimizer. The resolvent argument of lemma 12.6.9 and the normalized chord in a prescribed linear subspace give the completeness statement. The Iwasawa example comes with an explicit compact quotient and a proof, by averaging coefficients, that this quotient is not Kähler. The initial construction uses the normalized invariant probability measure. In dimension three, proposition 12.6.22, corollary 12.6.25 follow from the formula for the variation of mass proved in the book and from the polynomial continuity of bounded products. On the Iwasawa quotient, theorem 12.6.26 extends the determinant formula to probability measures invariant along the central fibers, by means of a closed equation on the base for the Schur complement. The exact vertical Dirichlet defect characterizes all maximizing smooth densities, and the completion estimates for this larger family concern the means of the coefficients of the minimizing forms.

For the warped cones in subsection 12.6.31, a closed equation on the base and an explicit balanced cofactor give the full quotient. The pullback of the affine Hessian metric becomes flat, and the variance of the trace at the endpoints gives the three alternatives: a strip, a half-plane or the whole plane. Smooth existence for the equation on the closed base is theorem 14.2.1, and integration fixes its scalar; the warped background on the product may be nonclosed. That the finite faces are not big is tested against closed top-degree forms on the base, so the conclusion applies to singular current representatives as well. In the computations on projective space and on periodic tori, the density and the cone are given explicitly throughout.

The cones of currents in proposition 12.6.43 are determined by localized closed test forms and Stokes' theorem for distributions. At the finite faces of the warped cone, proposition 12.6.44 applies theorem 14.19.2, the existence theorem for continuous solutions with $L^ p$ densities, on the closed base; it fixes the scalar by invariance of the mass under bounded perturbations and expands the pulled-back products. The obstruction to global $C^{1,1}$ solutions is the general bound of currents by determinants in proposition 5.28.6, derived from the identity for coefficients in proposition 5.28.5.

The convergence of the whole sequence in proposition 12.6.47 combines bounds for the reciprocal densities with the compactness for a fixed background in theorem 14.19.21. Since the base is closed, the uniqueness theorem for invariant mass, 14.25.2, identifies every cluster point of the potentials. For any bounded competitor at the endpoint pulled back from the base, the density forced away from the extreme set already exhausts the total mass of the closed class, so positivity excludes residual mass on that set before uniqueness is applied.

The alternatives for the trace in proposition 12.6.49, proposition 12.6.51 follow from the explicit balanced cofactor and from integrals of reciprocal squares over tubes, while the mass on the closed base controls the remaining cofactor term. When the trace diverges, its normalization concentrates on the extreme components where the ratio is minimal; if there is a single extreme point, the whole sequence converges to a fiber current. Both the smooth numerator and the denominator then tend to zero, while their quotient remains equal to one.

In section 12.12, bigness of the closed nef core with positive top self-intersection follows from Demailly and Păun's criterion [Theorem 0.5, DP04], as recalled in [SGPT]; no such criterion for arbitrary nonclosed nef backgrounds is used.

On the warped paths of section 12.13, the same balanced cofactor as in subsection 12.6.31 computes the cost for every minimizing test. The finite improper identity follows from the first variation and the actual nef limit, while the five rates of proposition 12.13.4 come from the first and second inverse moments of the fiber coefficient. The exclusion of every closed nef positive-volume core in proposition 12.13.6 uses the smooth-test obstruction to bigness and Demailly–Păun's [arXiv v2, Theorem 2.12, pp. 12–13, DP04], together with the global potential consequence of the Kähler $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma. The constant closed case gives exactly the expression in Tosatti's Morse inequality [v2, Theorem 1.1, p. 1, Tosatti26]; this comparison does not assign a closed cohomology class to a nonconstant warped coefficient.

In the radial model on a projective manifold in section 12.14, a global bounded potential compensates the coefficient along the fibers and gives the lower bound against every smooth Gauduchon test, and explicit balanced metrics give matching values after perturbation. The test against closed top-degree forms on the base in theorem 12.14.6 excludes every quasi-plurisubharmonic potential whose curvature current is strictly positive.
