This disproves the conjecture that positive volume implies bigness without further restrictions; its versions for closed forms and for surfaces remain separate questions.

The limits of test forms in subsection 12.14.9 are computed from these explicit balanced metrics by Stokes' theorem for closed forms and radial integration. In dimension three the powers normalized by the trace concentrate on the degenerate fiber at a logarithmic rate, whereas in higher dimension their threshold quotient stays positive. Localized closed forms on the base, with a small Kähler correction, give a different balanced family approaching the fiber in every dimension of the model.

The initial metric of the Chern–Ricci flow in 12.34.8 is chosen so that, up to a smooth global change of gauge, the radial background is the limiting form at the maximal time, and the maximal-time theorem determines this lifetime. In the normalization $\operatorname {Ric}=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \omega ^ n$, time one corresponds to time $1/(2\pi )$ for the Chern–Ricci form $-2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \omega ^ n$ used in this book. A test against a closed form on the base excludes every positive representative at later times, and the support and the vertical rank of all annihilators at the endpoint follow directly from the semipositive representative and the formula for the trace matrix. The averaged trace is a special case of the general identity for the flow proved before.

In the criteria of 12.10.22, invariance of the mass of bounded potentials and the support of the measure on the contact set prevent the stretched obstacle envelopes from collapsing, and the sublinear condition provides competitors. The uniform bound for Lelong numbers in lemma 5.38.8 then gives vanishing Lelong numbers by scaling. The argument with smooth roots of rank two extends the scalar first-order equation across the analytic set, and the support theorem for currents carried by analytic sets, recalled in section 5.38, removes its residual current. The calculations on Hopf manifolds and quadrics give examples in which the dual problem is attained. The general implications involving moments and entropy remain separate questions.

In the example with a point pole, proposition 12.10.33, radial integration shows directly that the potential has full mass, and the equality case of the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for matrices, combined with the local strong maximum principle, excludes every smooth semipositive maximizing test form. The argument does not need to identify the potential with the greatest threshold envelope. The thresholds for entropy and weighted integrability in corollary 12.10.35 follow directly from the computed radial density. They concern the density of this single equation, whereas the question of uniform moment or entropy conditions concerns the determinant-weighted probability measures of a maximizing sequence when the supremum is attained by a smooth semipositive test.

The bound for the determinant at the endpoint, theorem 12.9.2, is derived within the book from the criterion for mass invariance and the quotient by the lower mass; related criteria for the mass are [Propositions 3.2 and 3.3(iv), GL22]. The concentrating family in section 12.18 distinguishes the unique smooth maximizer for one density from maximizing sequences whose higher moments diverge.

The coordinate formula (12.18.7) identifies the intrinsic determinant measure on singular and degenerate positive currents. The proof of theorem 12.18.8 applies Tosatti and Weinkove's [arXiv v2, Corollary 1, p. 1, TW10] separately to each smooth positive root. The source uses $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \varphi $; the potential is multiplied by $2\pi $ here, and theorem 11.1.7 fixes the volume coefficient. The last paragraph of that source, p. 8, refers the existence argument to Cherrier and Demailly or the authors' earlier paper. No estimates uniform in the varying right-hand sides are used.

The closed and nonclosed torus families in theorem 12.18.13, theorem 12.18.15 preserve the complete determinant data and positive mass extrema while ellipticity degenerates. For the nonclosed family, the lower-power identities are verified on the two-coordinate block, retaining its fixed nonzero torsion. In theorem 12.18.17, the Poisson kernel gives uniformly convergent continuous potentials and exact maximizers for varying roots. The limiting current has rank-deficient absolutely continuous and singular coefficient parts, so its determinant measure vanishes although the bounded potential has positive Monge–Ampère mass. These calculations concern scalar perturbations and current limits; they supply no flow existence or convergence theorem.

The identity (12.17.3) of lemma 12.17.2, for bounded potentials in a background $g$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$, uses the calculus of bounded products and of weighted decreasing limits in proposition 5.28.2, lemma 5.27.2, whose classical local foundations are [Section 2, Theorems 2.1 and 2.4, pp. 4–9, BT82]. That the sign $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\leq 0$ gives positive lower mass is part of the criteria in terms of the sign of the torsion of Angella, Guedj and Lu [Theorem 3.2, pp. 4641–4642, AGL23]. The curvature calculation in theorem 12.17.7 identifies this sign on principal elliptic threefolds, and the two quotient constructions give explicit mass constants in the present convention for the operator. The conclusion for the determinant of the full current then follows from the endpoint theorem proved in the book and a change of background.

The estimate for local families in theorem 12.9.7 controls the solution form and its Gauduchon factor by two contractions. The elliptic input is the parametrix and Fredholm argument on compact manifolds in Taylor [Chapter 7, Sections 4 and 10, especially (10.4)–(10.6), Taylor7], together with the mapping properties on Hölder spaces in [Chapter 13, (8.7), (8.17) and (8.22), Taylor13]. Invariance of the index is [Section 7, Proposition 7.4, TaylorFA], and smooth regularity for nonlinear elliptic equations is also formulated in [Proposition, TaylorReg]. The estimates for the equation and for the normalized factor give explicit constants for the densities without assuming positive lower mass; instead, the data are restricted to smooth functions in a small $C^{2,\alpha }$ neighborhood.

The factor bound in proposition 12.9.15 starts from the conformal theorem of Gauduchon [Théorème 2 and its proof, pp. 132–133, GauduchonStandard85]. Its general statement has no restriction on the first Betti number; the even-Betti assumption belongs to the surface theorem at the beginning of that article. The smooth maximum principle is recalled and applied in [pp. 131–132, GauduchonStandard85]. The quantitative estimate here writes the cofactor equation in real divergence form and proves its Harnack bound by power iteration and a dyadic mean-oscillation argument. Since $d(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)=d\omega $, the vector coefficient is controlled by the fixed torsion. This supplies the exact-adjoint bounds of theorem 12.9.18 without derivative bounds on the varying solution form. Gauduchon uses $d^ c=\mathrm i(\bar\partial -\partial )$ and $L=-\operatorname {tr}(dd^ c)$; the positive factor equation is unchanged by this scaling and sign conversion.

The classical analytic input in section 12.22 is Hironaka's elimination of indeterminacies: every modification is dominated by a composition of blowups with smooth centers. The argument by principalization and domination is explained by Abramovich, Karu, Matsuki and Włodarczyk [Sections 1.2.3–1.2.4, pp. 538–539, and Section 5.4, p. 564, AKMW02], where the analytic case is treated explicitly. The curvature of the exceptional divisors then gives the uniform bound for the pairings used here; no factorization into a sequence of blowdowns is needed for this estimate.

For the fixed projective cones in section 12.25, every Gauduchon test is compared with a closed form of constant rank through an explicit logarithm of an exceptional divisor, which gives the exact loss of rank when the prescribed effective divisors are removed. For a general modification whose source is Kähler, proposition 12.25.11 obtains in addition two-sided bounds by powers from the intersection polynomial for closed backgrounds in section 12.20. Fixed coefficient functions that vanish, cones of residuals without restrictions, and sources that are not Kähler lie outside this construction.

The theorem that the line bundle of a smooth anticanonical curve of self-intersection zero is unitary flat near the curve, theorem 12.27.3, is due to Chen, Filip, Sun, Tosatti and Zhang [Theorem 1.1, with the standing degree-zero hypothesis in Section 1.1, CFSTZ26]. Its proof uses their identification of the holomorphic fibers in Proposition 4.1, the elliptic inverse independent of the holonomy in Lemma 5.2, and the weighted horizontal inverse and contraction of Propositions 5.4–5.5. The cutoff in proposition 12.27.5 is the construction at the end of their proof in Section 6. The variational bounds in rank one follow from proposition 12.26.1, and the examples obtained by blowing up nine points on a plane cubic, together with their torsion criterion, follow by restriction to the cubic. Only this local theorem and its direct consequences are used, not the global classification of surfaces in that paper.

The pencil in the case of finite holonomy and the rigidity in the non-torsion case, proposition 12.28.2, theorem 12.28.3, give the case of a smooth reduced divisor of Koike's [Lemma 3.5, Koike26]. The Levi-flat level sets of the flat norm have a smooth suspension model, so the density of their leaves and the maximum modulus argument are proved directly. The hypothesis is that the line bundle of the divisor is unitary flat near the smooth compact divisor; the global criteria for semipositivity and the dichotomy between fibrations and the Hartogs phenomenon in Koike's paper are not used. Together with the theorem on anticanonical neighborhoods, these local results explain the non-Stein and Hartogs properties of the nine-point examples with non-torsion normal bundle.

The quotient construction in proposition 12.29.3 follows the mechanism of invariant fibers of Denisi and Höring [v1, Lemma 2.10, p. 6, Proposition 4.2, p. 12 and pp. 14–18, and Theorem 5.1, p. 19, DH26]. Their action has $\kappa =2\pi \mathrm{i}\rho $, where $\kappa $ is the parameter of proposition 12.29.3 and $\rho $ is theirs, and their function $\mu _ Q$ equals $1+2\sigma $, with $\sigma $ the function defined before that proposition. The Laurent argument in lemma 12.29.1 proves directly the obstruction for punctured line bundles used in their Example 2.1, while example 12.29.2 computes the degree of an explicit factor of automorphy by its invariant metric. The statement about the quotient includes the two exceptional parameters, which are treated with compact elliptic curves. The computation of classes in theorem 12.30.4 gives their Proposition 4.2 and Lemmas 4.5 and 4.7–4.8, with explicit generators and conventions for projectivization. The flat unitary character in lemma 12.30.2 treats line bundles of every positive degree $d$ directly; the coefficient of the quotient is then $\kappa =2\pi \mathrm{i}d\rho $. This gives their non-Stein conclusion for split elliptic ruled surfaces without the reduction to a finite cover in their Lemma 5.2.

For the split elliptic ruled surface $M$, the algebra $\bigoplus _{r\geq 0}H^0(M,\operatorname {Sym}^ rT_ M)$ in theorem 12.31.4 has the bigness and nonfinite generation stated in [v1, Theorem 1.4, p. 2, with proof on pp. 9–10, DH26]. The decomposition by polynomial weights in lemma 12.31.1 gives the exact dimensions and the tautological volume in theorem 12.31.3, and its map to leading coefficients gives a direct proof of nonfinite generation through a quotient by an ideal of square zero. For canonical extensions, [v1, Remark 3.8, pp. 10–11, DH26] also states bigness and nonfinite generation, leaving the proof to the reader. The homogeneous quadric in lemma 12.32.1 and the decomposition of coefficients under the unipotent action give the description as a polynomial algebra in theorem 12.32.2. The exact dimensions, the tautological volume and nonfinite generation in corollary 12.32.3 follow for every extension class that is nonzero on the fibers of the ruling, including all Kähler canonical extensions on the split surface. The case of an extension class vanishing on the fibers of the ruling, proposition 12.33.2, follows directly from the ordinary cotangent quadric and the same decomposition of coefficients. Its section algebra is the same as in the case of nonzero restriction, while proposition 12.33.3 identifies the universal cover of the corresponding torsor, which is not Stein, as the product of $\mathbb C^2$ with the total space of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-2)$.

The question whether a weak Monge–Ampère power admits a scalar conformal factor is raised by Lu [Chapter 3, Section 5, LuHDR22]. The representation by finite currents in theorem 12.8.2 gives a supporting probability measure without defining that weak power or its scalar factor.

25.4 Positivity, Hermitian geometry, and volume

25.4 Closed classes and singular lociF9B38BEB0BCF

For closed classes on a Hermitian manifold, almost positive representatives keep the cohomology class separate from the auxiliary metric. The convention in section 10.11 follows Boucksom's thesis [Section 2.1.2, BouThesis02]; it does not assign a Bott–Chern class to a nonclosed Hermitian form.

The smooth and analytic regularizations of 5.36.3, used for proposition 10.12.2, have the lower bounds of [Theorem 2.1, Bou04Zariski]; see also [Theorems 1.2.9–1.2.10, BouThesis02]. Smooth regularization loses positivity by a multiple of a continuous approximation of the Lelong numbers, whereas analytic regularization has a curvature error tending uniformly to zero and does not increase Lelong numbers.

The minimal multiplicities of definition 10.12.1 are defined through these almost positive approximating families, as in [Definition 2.1.5, BouThesis02]. They must be distinguished from the Lelong numbers of a single current with minimal singularities: in the example of a nef class on a ruled surface in [Section 1.2.3, BouThesis02], a current with minimal singularities has nonzero Lelong numbers.

The non-Kähler locus of definition 10.13.1 is defined in [Definition 2.1.19, BouThesis02], and the proof of theorem 10.13.2 by finite intersections and regularized maxima is the argument of [Theorem 2.1.20, BouThesis02].

The equivalence between the existence of a Kähler current and the existence of a Kähler modification, used in section 10.10, is the classical criterion recalled in [Theorem 1.2.11, BouThesis02]; it is used as an external geometric input. The equality of the non-Kähler locus and the null locus of a nef and big class is the transcendental Nakamaye theorem of Collins and Tosatti [CT15Loci], which also holds on compact manifolds in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$; section 10.10 recalls this theorem from the literature.

Restricted volumes give a numerical test for these loci. The numerical restricted volume (10.14.1) follows Collins and Tosatti [Section 2, CT22Restricted]; the requirement that the analytic singularities have a smooth remainder is part of that definition.

The existence of Kähler models for every subvariety uses Fujiki's theorem that class $\mathcal C$ is closed under passing to closed subspaces [Lemma 4.6(2), Fujiki78], followed by Varouchas's theorem on Kähler modifications in the form stated and explained by Barlet [Theorem 10, pp. 31–32, Barlet00]. A common Kähler refinement is obtained by embedded resolution of the graph in a Kähler product, using Bierstone and Milman [Theorem 1.6 and Remark 1.7(2), BM97]. These are classical geometric inputs. The descent of potentials is proved in proposition 5.43.18, so the proof of mass invariance does not repeat it.

In proposition 10.16.5, positive non-pluripolar mass implies bigness by [Proposition 1.22, BEGZ10]. The definition of the positive product, its agreement with the cup product for nef classes, and the fact that it is attained by currents with minimal singularities are in [Definition 1.17, arXiv pp. 17–18, and Proposition 1.20, arXiv p. 20, BEGZ10]. The normalized diagonal current (10.16.7) uses the mass-concentration theorem of Demailly and Păun [Proposition 2.6, DP04] and makes explicit the coefficient in the construction of [Theorem 2.12, DP04]. These results on Kähler manifolds are used as classical inputs. The identity for the mass with a bounded residual in lemma 10.17.3, by contrast, follows directly from the book's formula for bounded masses, by comparison of polynomials. The comparison with the numerical restricted volume for nef classes is [Lemma 2.6, CT22Restricted], and the final equality in (10.16.11) uses the theorem [Theorem 1.1, CT15Loci] recalled above.

The rigidity criterion for nef boundary classes on tori, theorem 10.26.1, develops the flat model of Fu and Ouyang [v1, Section 3, pp. 5–6, FuOuyang26]. Testing against Fourier modes proves the vanishing along the kernel directly, and the metric argument uses a finite covering by dense leaves and a character of the circle. The collapse in this theorem is along a fixed positive perturbation $\theta +t\kappa $, where $\kappa $ is a translation-invariant Kähler form. The calculation with mixed forms in example 10.26.3 shows that the clause in their Lemma 3.1 and Proposition 3.2 allowing arbitrary approaching classes cannot be used in that generality; their Theorem 4.4, which concerns positive perturbations, and the distinction made in their Remark 6.4, p. 18, concern a different setting. Their general theorems on collapse, fibrations and lattice dynamics for K3 surfaces are not used in this argument on tori.

The nonrigid class with an irrational ray in proposition 10.27.2 is the explicit Kummer construction of [v1, Section 7.1, pp. 18–19, proof of Theorem 1.4(a), FuOuyang26]. The resolution of the quotient and its Kähler metric are described in local charts, and the difference of two representatives is given an explicit periodic global $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-primitive. Periods over translated real two-dimensional subtori detect the irrational ray without extending cohomology classes across the punctures. Fu and Ouyang's conclusions about diameters of Ricci-flat metrics, spectra and limit spaces require additional inputs and are not used in this construction.

The family obtained from four points and its central metric in section 10.28 are Qin's construction [v1, Theorem A, p. 1, and Section 3, Lemmas 3.1–3.3, pp. 3–4, QinMetricExtension26]. Qin's proof of the nonextension theorem on p. 5 uses global $L^2$ extension for adjoint bundles. Theorem 10.28.4 instead uses the conics of degree zero of lemma 10.28.3: Fubini's theorem, averages over disks and Harnack's inequality force the central weights to be harmonic away from the node, and the remaining curvature has logarithmic coefficient one, whereas the metric constructed here has coefficient one half. This shows that the metric has no semipositive extension whose central restriction is at most as singular as the metric itself, without using global adjoint extension and without asserting that this metric has minimal singularities. Varying the conic gives the exact set of restrictions in theorem 10.28.9: the divisor metric of the negative line multiplied by the pullback of an arbitrary semipositive metric on the base of the pencil. The converse is constructed from the two homogeneous sections of the pencil, and corollary 10.28.10 concerns the least singular metrics among these restrictions.

Inoue surfaces were introduced by Inoue [Inoue74], and their higher-dimensional analogues by Oeljeklaus and Toma [OT05], who proved that the action of $\mathcal O_ K\rtimes U$ used in section 10.29 is free, properly discontinuous and cocompact, and that the resulting manifolds are not Kähler. Ornea and Verbitsky showed that Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds with $t=1$ contain no positive-dimensional complex subvarieties, using a semipositive closed form with dense null leaves [OV11OT]. The decomposition of Inoue surfaces into three-dimensional tori filled by dense leaves, and a Liouville argument along the leaves for bounded harmonic functions, appear in the work of Fang, Tosatti, Weinkove and Zheng on the Chern–Ricci flow [Section 2, Lemma 2.1, FTWZ16], where the Tricerri metric and the identity $\mathrm{Ric}(\omega _ T)=-\alpha $ are also recorded; their form $\alpha =\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d\overline w/(4y^2)$ equals $2\pi \theta $ in the normalization of section 10.29, and their $\omega _ T=4\alpha +\beta $ is the Tricerri metric used there. The description of all $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions in theorem 10.29.4, the mass computations of proposition 10.29.10 and the absence of plurisigned metrics in proposition 10.29.14 are proved directly here. Angella, Guedj and Lu proved that, on a compact threefold, a Hermitian metric with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \geq 0$ gives finite upper mass and one with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$ gives positive lower mass; in particular a pluriclosed metric gives both [Theorem B, AGL23]. The general question of finiteness and positivity of these masses is [Problem 1.8, AGL23]. Angella, Dubickas, Otiman and Stelzig showed that an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold admits a pluriclosed metric only if $s=t$ [Corollary 3, ADOS24]; proposition 10.29.14 shows that for type $(s,1)$ with $s\geq 2$ there is not even a metric whose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ has a sign.

25.6 Monge–Ampère and complex Hessian equations

25.6 Smooth and continuous equationsE1BC130DDD5C

On a Hermitian manifold, the smooth Monge–Ampère equation determines a normalization constant together with the potential. For $n\geq 2$, the existence theorem theorem 14.2.1 is Tosatti and Weinkove's [Corollary 1, TW10]. Their equation, for a smooth function $F$ prescribing the logarithm of the density, is written with $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \varphi $; the substitution $u=2\pi \varphi $ gives the convention of this book, and a prescribed smooth volume form $\mathrm dV$ is absorbed by replacing $F$ with $F+\log (\mathrm dV/\omega ^ n)$. The concavity argument with Gauduchon metrics for the normalization constant in theorem 14.8.1 also appears in Collins's [Theorem 2.13, Collins21].

The proof of the uniform estimate for the potential in section 14.1 by weighted integration follows Cherrier and Tosatti–Weinkove [Cherrier87, TW10]: a finite recurrence absorbs the torsion terms before the Sobolev iteration. The calculation of the torsion terms in the second-order estimate of section 14.1 goes back to Cherrier; its form with completed squares and the maximum-principle argument follow [Sections 3 and 9, TW15].

The interpolation in lemma 14.5.7 is the mechanism of Jiaogen Zhang and Xi Zhang's [v1, Proposition 4.1 and its proof, p. 16, ZhangHessianInterpolation26]. The fixed scalar operator is uniformly elliptic for a Hermitian metric as well, so the linear implication here does not require closedness. Their nonlinear Hessian application assumes a Kähler metric and a small product of its negative bisectional-curvature bound with the solution's oscillation. Its argument for data close to one in $L^1$ uses a stability estimate with $q>n/k$ and a uniform $L^ q$ bound; the smallness threshold depends on that bound. The interpolation lemma supplies neither this nonlinear trace estimate nor an arbitrary-$L^1$ stability criterion.

Prescribing the volume form of a Gauduchon metric leads to a different equation, which contains first-order torsion terms. The existence theorem theorem 14.10.1 is due to Székelyhidi, Tosatti and Weinkove [Theorem 1.4, STW17], again with the potential multiplied by $2\pi $. The bound for the potential in section 14.11 follows Székelyhidi's [Propositions 10–11 and Remark 12, Sze18], specialized to the determinant of the Gauduchon equation, and the second-order argument in section 14.14 follows [Section 3, STW17]. The identities (14.13.4), taken from [Section 4, STW17], explain the structure of the first-order perturbation.

The gradient estimate combines a blow-up argument with a Liouville theorem. In (14.16.3), where $A_ j$ are the rescaling factors of the blow-up, the first-order term is kept before rescaling and tends to zero at the rate $A_ j^{-1}$, as in [Section 6, Sze18]. The Euclidean argument in section 14.15 specializes [Theorem 20, Sze18] to the Gauduchon cone. Once the equation is uniformly elliptic, lemma 14.17.1 uses the Evans–Krylov theorem for variable coefficients of Tosatti, Wang, Weinkove and Yang [Definition 3.2 and Theorem 3.4, TWWY15].

For densities in $L^ p$, the existence of continuous solutions of the equation with a normalization constant (theorem 14.19.2) and of the exponential equation (14.19.4) is due respectively to Kołodziej and Nguyen [Theorem 0.1, KN15] and to Nguyen [Theorem 0.1, Nguyen16]. Their operator is twice the one used here: for the exponent $\lambda >0$ in (14.19.4), the conversion is $u=2\varphi $, where $\varphi $ is their solution, and the exponent in their equation is $2\lambda $. These results require neither bounded mass nor positive lower volume. Compactness comes from local capacity estimates: the arguments of [Section 5, KN15] and [Section 6, Dinew16] lead to theorem 14.19.21, which is the statement of [Corollary 5.10, KN15]. A common bound for the densities is essential here; the $L^1$ compactness of normalized potentials alone does not suffice.

For measures satisfying a power bound in capacity, Kołodziej and Nguyen [Proposition 2.4, pp. 2954–2956, KNHolder18] give stability measured against the Monge–Ampère measure of the solution. The thin-sublevel estimate and backwards iteration of lemma 14.19.14, lemma 14.19.16 follow the capacity argument in [v2, Theorem 5.3 and Lemma 5.4, pp. 10–12, KN15], using their modified comparison theorem [v2, Theorem 2.3, pp. 5–6, KN15]. The geometric iteration in the book covers every power $1+\alpha $, $\alpha >0$, including the total-capacity endpoint. Choosing the sublevel height proportional to the cube of the comparison reserve gives the exponent $\alpha /[3n(1+\alpha )+\alpha ]$ in proposition 14.19.23; the square-capacity case has exponent $1/(6n+1)$. The measure can be singular. The preprint [v2, p. 1, KN15] uses $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /\pi $, twice our operator; its backgrounds become $2\omega $ with the same potentials, and its top products acquire the factor $2^ n$.

The threshold equation in theorem 15.33.1 combines this iteration with bounded-density solvability and the full Gauduchon formula. Local $L^1$ compactness uses Demailly's Propositions 4.21 and 5.9 [Chapter I, pp. 36–37 and 40, DemCADG]. The weighted local product estimate is Nguyen's [v1, Proposition 1.1, pp. 5–6, Nguyen16]; uniform continuity of bounded products is Bedford and Taylor's [Corollary 2.8 and Theorem 2.10, p. 10, BT82]. For a Hermitian background, the local closed product must still be expanded with every smooth correction factor, as in proposition 5.28.2. The logarithmic construction in theorem 15.33.6 uses the exponential volume–capacity estimate (5.29.3) and gives a datum outside every higher $L^ p$ class with an exact continuous threshold solution. The added capacity hypothesis leaves the general root-tail and exact-equation questions open.

For a continuous solution whose measure is dominated by a Hölder reference, theorem 15.5.4 combines the weighted Chern estimate with the square-capacity stability. The coordinated transform parameter and comparison reserve keep the minimizing radii comparable to the smoothing radius. The resulting exponent is sufficient for the range theorem; no optimal exponent is asserted. The argument assumes continuity of the solution.

The smoothness theorem theorem 14.19.32 is the strictly positive, globally smooth-data case of Badiane, Lu and Zeriahi's [v1, Theorem 1.1, p. 2; Section 4.2, p. 17, BLZBoundedSmooth26]. Their auxiliary second-order estimate is Proposition 4.1, pp. 13–17. The square of the prescribed potential in lemma 14.19.31 absorbs the derivatives of the frozen density, and bounded exponential comparison identifies the uniform limit with the original solution. The argument then uses the concave uniformly elliptic extension of the logarithmic determinant and the Evans–Krylov theorem for variable coefficients [Definition 3.2, Theorem 3.4, and the paragraph following it, TWWY15]. Only the strictly positive Hermitian background and global smooth positive density are treated here; the primary paper also considers degenerate backgrounds and data with a singular regular locus.

The exponential term gives a comparison principle even when the densities have no positive lower bound; lemma 14.19.28 recovers [Lemma 2.3, Nguyen16]. Letting the exponent tend to zero then identifies the normalization constant through (14.19.35), as in [Corollary 0.2, Nguyen16]. This proves uniqueness of the constant, but not uniqueness of the limiting potential. The weighted mean (14.19.27), taken from [Proposition 2.5, Nguyen16], controls the normalization; here its lower bound follows directly from the estimate for sublevel sets.

Equations with prescribed singularities require relative envelopes and separate assumptions on the reference potential and on the ambient metric. The results of Alehyane–Lu–Salouf and of Xuan Li [ALS26, XL26] are therefore treated separately in section 15.1, section 15.37, section 10.31; their sources are discussed in section 25.6.

For fully nonlinear concave equations, the uniform estimate under a quantitative subsolution condition is due to Guo and Phong [v1, Theorem 3.1 and its proof, pp. 8–11, GP24]. The strict asymptotic gap of an admissible reference, the matrix bound, the linear stability estimate and the uniform compactness in subsection 14.19.42 follow Guo and Song [v1, Lemma 2.1, Proposition 2.8 and Lemma 2.9, pp. 4–11, GS26]. In the book, the zero-order estimate uses the real contact-set construction of proposition 14.11.1, and theorem 14.19.19 bounds both the auxiliary potential and its normalization constant; with these inputs the constants do not depend on a positive lower bound for the right-hand sides. Writing the potential of these sources as $u/(2\pi )$ converts their convention for smooth curvature forms into the normalization of this book.

The gradient estimate in subsection 14.19.47 is Guo and Song's [v1, Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 3.1 with Lemmas 3.2–3.6, pp. 11–17, GS26]; the earlier alternative for convex level sets is Székelyhidi's [arXiv v3, Propositions 5–6, pp. 5–7, Sze18]. The tangent-hyperplane argument in lemma 14.19.48 uses the common strict gap to keep the constants uniform at every positive level. The differentiation is carried out for $U=u/(2\pi )$, where $u$ is the solution, and the final finite net of smooth comparison functions is provided by corollary 14.19.46.

25.6 Monge–Ampère and complex Hessian equations

25.6 Uniqueness and selectionE1BC130DDD5C

When the exponent is zero, uniqueness of the normalization constant leaves open the separate question of uniqueness of the potential. Degeneration of the density affects comparison, whereas the family of equations with positive exponent can select a particular solution of the critical equation. The argument by concentration of mass for densities restricted to a set, around (14.25.6), follows Lu, Phung and Tô [proof of Theorem 3.7 and Remark 3.8, LPT20]. The exterior-ball argument for (14.22.11) instead propagates the maximum, following Bardi and Goffi [Proposition 2.4 and Theorem 2.5 in the cited preprint, BG18].

The uniqueness theorem for bounded potentials, theorem 14.24.1, concerns a continuous nonnegative density whose positivity set is connected and dense, and is proved with energy estimates on level sets and auxiliary test potentials. The mixed inequality and the passage to coefficient densities use the local calculus of section 5.21, and the continuity of bounded solutions is obtained in the book itself, by a comparison argument, in corollary 14.19.29. The smooth local Dirichlet problem needed for proposition 14.24.13 is solved by Guan's theorem [Theorem 1.1, pp. 687–688, Guan98], whose hypothesis is satisfied by a strictly plurisubharmonic quadratic subsolution. The estimate on the real contact set then gives a constant that depends only on the fixed geometry and the $L^2$ bound, and not on the height of the test density.

For measurable densities that are bounded above and bounded away from zero, uniqueness is derived in corollary 14.24.17 from the same energy argument on level sets. The classical counterpart is [Corollary 3.9 and Remark 3.13, KN19], where the locators refer to the authors' version indicated in the bibliography.

25.6 Monge–Ampère and complex Hessian equations

25.6 Complex Hessian equationsE1BC130DDD5C

The cone inequalities and the estimate with a prescribed potential in section 8.1 follow Fang's [v1, Lemma 2.2, Proposition 2.3 and Theorem 3.1, pp. 5–6 and 8–17, FangHessianSmooth26]. The scalar shift in 8.2.3 is proved through real roots, including its endpoint. Polarized positivity then gives the mixed-trace and linearized coefficient bounds. The largest-eigenvalue argument keeps the Chern torsion terms and evaluates every derivative of the Hessian root at the original matrix, while a separate positive perturbation supplies its smooth lower support. In the quadratic weight used for the potential, the bound $-3A\leq \Psi '\leq -A$ determines the choice of the small eigenvalue parameter. The absolute mixed-form estimate below Hessian degree $m$ and the torsion bounds for products are the mechanisms of Kołodziej and Nguyen [arXiv v2, Section 2.1, pp. 4–7, KNHessian16].

The Euclidean Liouville theorem 8.3.2 is due to Dinew and Kołodziej [arXiv v2, Theorem 3.2, pp. 8–11, DKHessian17]. Their rescaling argument is Section 2, pp. 6–7, there; its Hermitian version is also used by Székelyhidi [arXiv v2, Section 6, pp. 26–27, Sze18]. The proof here uses constant-cone linear tests and lower viscosity tests to pass to the maximal limit, so it does not require a variable-background Hessian-product convergence theorem. The averaging proof obtains the uniform directional energy bound with a fixed dependence on the smaller averaging radius. The subsequent local Laplace estimate controls the real Hessian in finite $L^ p$ spaces.

Smooth proper existence and admissible approximation are the mechanisms of Kołodziej and Nguyen [arXiv v2, Theorem 3.17 and Lemma 3.20, pp. 23–25, KNHessian16] and Guedj and Lu [arXiv v1, Theorem 1.7, pp. 4–5, GLHessian25]. Here the smooth trace and gradient estimates first close the proper continuity path. Its penalty equations then approximate every continuous admissible potential uniformly. This construction precedes the definition of continuous Hessian products and does not use a domination theorem. For positive exponential coefficient $a$, rescaling both the metric and the potential reduces the equation to coefficient one. The maximum comparison in 8.8.1 gives the coefficient $a^{-1}$ for continuous data. The existence assertion in 8.8.3 then follows from a contraction on the interval between constant barriers, followed by the continuous regularity theorem.

The decreasing approximation theorem 8.6.6 extends the construction to bounded potentials and recovers Kołodziej and Nguyen's [arXiv v2, Lemma 3.20, pp. 25–26, KNHessian16]. The bounded upper-test characterization is the one used by Guedj and Lu [arXiv v1, Section 1.1.1, pp. 3–4, GLHessian25], through smooth strictly elliptic linear tests. Here successive smooth obstacles are chosen below the preceding admissible approximant, and the penalty error is then made smaller than their fixed gap. This gives a decreasing sequence before defining any product of the bounded potential. The same squeeze proves 8.7.4 after the continuous obstacle envelope has been constructed.

Continuous mixed products and their uniform continuity are [arXiv v2, Proposition 2.11 and Corollary 2.12, pp. 10–11, KNHessian16]. The contact comparison, nonvanishing and domination arguments of section 8.7 follow Guedj and Lu [arXiv v1, Lemma 1.10, Theorems 2.1–2.2 and Corollaries 2.3–2.4, pp. 6 and 8–9, GLHessian25]. The continuous obstacle envelope is constructed by the same penalty solutions, giving continuity and contact support directly. Differentiated background factors are interpreted using the signed lower-degree products. In the mass nonvanishing proof, the telescoping form has degree $n-1$ and retains each power of the original potential. The normalized linear Green estimate rules out an open set on which the stretched difference envelopes tend to $-\infty $.

The bounded recursion in section 8.9 follows the construction of Kołodziej and Nguyen [Lemmas 3.1–3.2, Theorem 3.3 and Proposition 3.7, pp. 125–129, KNHermitianMeasures26]. Their local cone is imposed on $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, whereas the book imposes it on $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. The proof here therefore expands each raw factor into a shifted admissible factor minus the smooth background before applying the coefficient estimates. The first limit is in the first potential, and the final limit is in the last potential; the top unwedged current remains distributional. The positive shifted wedge has measure coefficients, while its background derivatives are given explicitly in 8.9.7. Permutation invariance does not follow from this ordered construction alone, as the source also points out in [Remark 3.6, p. 128, KNHermitianMeasures26]. Its later capacity and weighted-convergence results concern the source local class. The elementary correction in 8.9.8 places $u+\rho $ in that class while retaining the same Hermitian metric. It preserves the nonclosed background terms and does not itself prove the capacity quasicontinuity needed for higher-degree simultaneous convergence.

The two-factor argument in section 8.10 uses instead the global conformal Gauduchon multiplier of theorem 11.4.2. The energy identity for $u^2$ bounds the Sobolev norm, and first-order integration by parts retains the $\mathrm dT$ term of the nonclosed Gauduchon test. Sobolev truncation and mollification prove the capacity bound for the positive linear trace; the second-cone inequality transfers it to every first-Hessian coefficient. Tail convex combinations from Mazur's lemma identify quasicontinuity with the canonical potential pointwise. A common exceptional set, Dini's theorem and bounded continuous extension then give the weighted convergence used in 8.10.5. This argument controls two factors without applying the source's local capacity results to a shifted cone. The cutoff absolute-coordinate potentials in 8.10.7 show that a two-Hessian measure can charge a smooth real codimension-two set of zero Sobolev capacity. Thus this capacity estimate cannot supply the higher-degree argument.

The local capacity and decreasing-convergence conclusions are studied in [Corollaries 3.18–3.19, p. 137, and Lemma 5.1, pp. 143–145, KNHermitianMeasures26]. In section 8.11, smooth competitors suffice to control the coefficients of the book's ordered currents. A fixed regularized maximum localizes decreasing smooth approximations near the boundary. The smooth energy variation retains every derivative of the Hermitian background and gives convergence in these local capacities. Outer-open coefficient estimates and bounded continuous extension then prove the weighted convergence needed for 8.11.12. This proof uses the global approximation already established in the chapter and avoids an identification of gradients in a singular weighted Sobolev completion. It gives decreasing convergence for the book's shifted class. At degree $m$ the unwedged current converges in distributions, while its positive wedge $Q_ m$ converges as a Radon measure.

The coefficient estimate in 8.2.8 uses Newton's inequality on the list with two coordinates deleted. A related bound appears in [equation (2-8), p. 111, KNHermitianMeasures26]. The torsion estimate at degree $m-1$ corresponds to [Lemma 2.4 and Corollary 2.5, pp. 113–114, KNHermitianMeasures26]. Its proof sums the diagonal wedge coefficients before taking absolute values and compares them with the positive gradient coefficients. This extends the smooth capacity induction to degree $m$. Positive shifted currents are then dominated by the corrected local Hessian traces, and 8.11.14 gives the weighted decreasing convergence studied in [Lemma 5.1(b), pp. 144–145, KNHermitianMeasures26]. The unwedged $D_ m$ retains its distributional meaning.

The strict locality and maximum inequality in 8.12.1, 8.12.2 correspond to [Corollary 5.2, p. 145, KNHermitianMeasures26], which concerns local unshifted Hessian products. The arguments here apply to the book's global shifted products. Continuous functions of decreasing potentials supply the strict-set cutoffs; a decreasing constant shift includes the contact set in the measure inequality.

The torsion-weight identity in 8.12.4 extends the smooth integration-by-parts argument using the coefficient capacity $c_{m-1}$. In 8.12.5, it allows the truncation argument of 8.7.6 to apply to bounded potentials on arbitrary Hermitian backgrounds. This is positivity of each individual mass; it does not supply a uniform positive lower bound over the admissible class.

The bounded mass formula in 8.13.1 extends the integration-by-parts calculation of theorem 11.1.5 using the recursive currents. The necessity argument in 8.13.4 is the polarization mechanism of [Theorems 1–2, Chiose16], used above in theorem 11.1.7. At Hessian degree $m$, only the powers $n-m,\ldots ,n-1$ occur. Sufficiency follows from the mixed maximum inequality, while 8.13.3 keeps the exact total-mass difference on arbitrary backgrounds. The example in 8.13.5 extends the smooth varying-mass torus calculation of example 11.1.12.

The mixed torsion comparison and weak modified comparison in 8.13.7, 8.13.8 use the mechanism of Gu and Nguyen [Lemmas 3.8–3.10, pp. 1197–1200, GuNguyenBoundary18]. Their local bounded-product construction uses a locally conformal Kähler reference metric. Here the global decreasing approximation and weighted torsion currents give the integration-by-parts identity for the chapter's shifted products. A finite mixed-degree induction controls the error by diagonal traces; rescaling the upper potential then absorbs the lower traces on a sufficiently small sublevel set.

The pointwise order in 8.2.10 uses the canonical linear subharmonic representatives of the admissible class. The positive volume term from 8.12.3 and weak modified comparison prove 8.13.10, 8.13.11 on arbitrary Hermitian backgrounds. The same strict comparison proves the logarithmic-data estimate in 8.13.12 for a fixed finite Radon right-hand measure. Together with smooth proper existence, it identifies the bounded solution in 8.13.13 without a separate continuity argument. The continuous-potential domination results in 8.7.7, 8.7.8 use the earlier envelope argument.

The conclusion of 8.8.2 is the continuous-solution case of Fang's [v1, Theorem 4.1, pp. 17–19, FangHessianSmooth26]. The theorem here assumes continuity of the given admissible weak solution; Fang's statement treats bounded solutions and also invokes a continuity result for them. The uniformly elliptic concave extension uses only a bounded complex Hessian. Its regularity input is the continuous-viscosity version of the Evans–Krylov–Caffarelli estimate in Tosatti, Wang, Weinkove and Yang [arXiv v2, Theorem 3.4 and the paragraph following it, pp. 16–20, TWWY15]. It applies directly to the auxiliary limit. The general bounded-solution continuity theory and results for degenerate backgrounds are separate from this argument.

25.6 Monge–Ampère and complex Hessian equations

25.6 Equations with prescribed singularitiesE1BC130DDD5C

Relative envelopes allow the solution of an equation to keep prescribed singularities while the measure on the right-hand side changes. Equations with $L^ p$ data in a prescribed ordinary type, equations with general measures, and equations under mass bounds on the metric use this framework in different ways. They differ both in the estimates available and in the singularity type of the solution obtained.

25.6 Monge–Ampère and complex Hessian equations

25.6 Equations of prescribed ordinary typeE1BC130DDD5C

The equations of prescribed ordinary type in theorem 15.12.1 are [Theorems 5.4 and 5.7, ALS26]. Replacing their reference volume $\omega ^ n$ by $\mathrm{d}V$ multiplies the density by a smooth positive function and preserves its $L^ p$ class, and a change of the normalization of the complex Hessian by a positive constant is absorbed by rescaling both the potential and the exponent.

The two constructions of [Lemmas 5.5–5.6, ALS26] are the relative estimate theorem 15.12.3 and the rooftop supersolution lemma 15.12.4; together they keep the solution in the ordinary type of the reference. For a big background, the argument with bounded subsolutions of Guedj and Lu [Lemma 3.3 and Theorem 3.4, GL23E] gives lemma 15.3.1, theorem 15.3.3.

The trace calculation with a barrier in section 15.19 follows Guyett and Mc Gowan [v1, Proposition 3.2, pp. 7–12, GM26]. Their geometric setting is a small crepant resolution, in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, of a normal projective Calabi–Yau variety, and their abstract Theorem 3.1 treats a closed semipositive big background with an upper bound for the mass. In the book, the arguments with bounded subsolutions and exponential comparison of lemma 15.3.1, theorem 15.3.3 give uniform bounds for the potentials and the scalars when the density is a fixed smooth positive function. The trace argument keeps the torsion of the perturbation and also allows a fixed nonzero Chern–Ricci form. Its conclusion is convergence of the potentials along subsequences, in a semipositive background with an explicit strict analytic barrier. The assertions of that paper about metric completions and conifold contractions are not part of this argument.

The bundle and the contraction in 15.19.8 form the standard model of a node used in [v1, Equation (2.1), p. 4, and Section 4, pp. 15–16, GM26]. The logarithmic curvature identity (15.19.11) gives a strict barrier for this model directly, and a cutoff in a positive collar makes it global. This proves the convergence of the potentials and the assertion about the area of the exceptional curves for these local resolutions, without using a classification of small resolutions or a theorem on metric completions. Since the canonical bundle is torsion, its local holomorphic trivializations give the Chern–Ricci-flat density.

The equation on the singular space, (15.19.16), is obtained through the general correspondence of theorem 9.11.5 between potentials on a resolution and potentials on the singular space defined by disk inequalities. For closed backgrounds, the identification in [v1, Lemma 3.1 and the proof of Corollary 1.1, pp. 13–14, GM26] uses the equation on normal spaces and the estimate for adapted measures of Eyssidieux, Guedj and Zeriahi [arXiv v2, Theorem 6.3 and Lemma 6.4, pp. 28–29, EGZ09]. In the standard model of a node, (15.19.15) gives in lemma 15.19.14 the exact range $p<3$ of integrability and the weak $L^3$ endpoint, for every smooth positive density on the resolution. The bounded energy identity already used in theorem 9.11.43 proves theorem 15.19.17, using smooth strict positivity only away from the exceptional curves.

The arguments for the metric completion and the distance in lemma 15.19.21, proposition 15.19.22 are those of [v1, Lemma 5.2, pp. 23–24, and Proposition 5.1, pp. 24–26, GM26]. Compact collars in the regular part separate the points added in the completion, and the first and last visits of a path to the finitely many contracting regions give a distance error controlled by these regions; uniform convergence of the metrics on each compact subset of the regular part suffices. The hypotheses on the diameters of punctured neighborhoods in the limit and on the intrinsic diameters for the approximating metrics are stated explicitly; the conifold estimates and the asymptotics of cones needed to verify them are separate geometric inputs.

For curves, [v1, Lemma 4.1, p. 17, GM26] bounds the diameter of $\mathbb P^1$ by a multiple of $A^{1/3}$, where $A$ is the area, under a uniform upper bound for the metric. Averaging over straight coordinate segments and splitting the kernel given by the reciprocal of the distance give the sharper logarithmic estimate of lemma 15.19.24 on every fixed compact Riemann surface. The radial example in example 15.19.25 has the same order, and rescaling it shows that the area alone does not control the diameter. The two radial paths and the connection through the zero section in proposition 15.19.26 give the mechanism of [v1, Proposition 4.2, pp. 20–21, GM26], with the uniform bound on the restriction to the curve and the radial bounds stated as explicit hypotheses.

Strict singular barriers extend the comparison argument to potentials with minimal singularities. The development starting in section 15.13 follows [Section 4, BGL25], where the bounded mass assumption of the earlier sections of that paper is dropped. The equations with minimal singularities, culminating in theorem 15.16.7, are [Theorems 4.6–4.7, BGL25]. The solution has finite mass, although the masses in its ordinary singularity type are not assumed to be uniformly bounded.

25.6 Monge–Ampère and complex Hessian equations

25.6 General measures in semipositive backgroundsE1BC130DDD5C

The local decomposition of measures used in lemma 5.27.10 is Cegrell's [Theorem 6.3, Ceg98], on a bounded hyperconvex domain in dimension at least two; for a non-pluripolar measure its pluripolar part vanishes. The global constructions in lemma 15.24.4, proposition 15.24.1 patch these local representations together.

The bounded-subsolution theorem theorem 15.10.1, taken from [Theorem 5.1, ALS26], solves the exponential equation whose right-hand side has a bounded density with respect to the Monge–Ampère measure of a bounded potential. Truncating the density in such a representation of a general measure brings this theorem into the construction for general measures, and domination then allows passage to the limit. The domination theorem for finite measures, theorem 15.37.6 in section 15.37, is [Theorem 3.14, ALS26]: the fixed finite measure prevents collapse, whereas the other members of the envelope class need not have finite mass. The proof of theorem 15.37.10 also allows the measure being compared to be infinite. The singular strict domination principle, theorem 15.2.2, follows [Theorem 3.11, ALS26].

The homogeneous range result theorem 15.25.1 is the sufficient direction of Kołodziej and Nguyen's [Theorem 1.3, p. 2952; proof pp. 2958–2963, KNHolder18]. Their weighted regularization estimate is [Lemma 2.8, p. 2957, KNHolder18]. The proof here first approximates a Borel density by continuous functions and then chooses smooth references diagonally. Common Hölder bounds give uniform capacity estimates and a weighted modulus for the varying solution measures; bounds above and below for the normalization constants prevent degeneration before the uniform limit is taken.

The radial bounded product in lemma 5.27.25 is a direct Bedford–Taylor calculation: the logarithmic derivative of a smooth radial maximum fixes the spherical mass. Summing these local references with geometric weights and controlling a common cutoff gives proposition 15.26.2. The homogeneous range theorem yields corollary 15.26.3, with a normalized Hölder solution and an unknown positive coefficient. The bounded-reference theorem yields theorem 15.26.4 for bounded densities against the fixed spherical probability, including singular data on backgrounds with zero lower mass. This is an individual geometric sufficient condition, distinct from solvability for every non-pluripolar measure and from the exact density-threshold question.

Passing to the limit in the measures requires that the lower envelopes do not collapse. The continuity theorem for measures dominated by a fixed measure, theorem 15.37.19, is [Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.1, condition (2), ALS26]; in this case positive lower mass prevents collapse, and no upper bound on the mass is used. The argument with a common envelope preceding corollary 15.37.24 gives instead the first alternative of [Lemma 4.2, ALS26]. When the approximants have the ordinary singularity type of the reference, this alternative needs no assumption of positive lower volume.

A common barrier in the ordinary singularity type also gives corollary 15.9.4, the corresponding case of [Theorem 4.1, ALS26]. The reference need not be an envelope fixed point; the condition in a smaller background suffices. Integrals of bounded potentials against varying mixed measures are handled by the torsion calculation in lemma 5.44.7, which follows Kołodziej and Nguyen [Lemma 2.3, KN22].

The resulting equations with general finite non-pluripolar measures, theorem 15.37.4, are [Theorem 5.8 and Corollary 5.9, ALS26]. The constructions with a minimal and with a prescribed reference in subsection 15.37.27, subsection 15.37.30 use the approximations of the density from that proof, and they assume both the condition (16.28.67) in a smaller background and positive lower mass. The solutions have finite mass, but for arbitrary measures they need not differ boundedly from the reference. For a Hermitian background and the minimal reference, corollary 15.37.32 identifies the scalar in the equation with the density threshold of theorem 15.28.4, that is, the largest coefficient for which the scaled density admits a subsolution. The question that remains, 24.2.2 in section 24.1, concerns zero lower mass. The weighted addition theorem theorem 15.11.1 is [Theorem 5.2, ALS26]; the proof given here localizes the passage to the equation.

25.6 Monge–Ampère and complex Hessian equations

25.6 Big backgrounds under mass boundsE1BC130DDD5C

Li's theory of equations with general measures [Theorems 6.1–6.2 and Corollary 6.1, XL26] assumes that the manifold has bounded mass and that the Hermitian metric has positive lower mass. It gives theorem 10.31.3 and the constructions with a model reference in subsection 10.31.43. Under bounded mass, positivity of the lower volume of the model reference implies that the metric has positive lower mass, so expressing the hypothesis through the reference reorganizes this setting without enlarging it.

The relative foundations of this theory use the domination, stretching and obstacle estimates discussed in section 25.4. In (10.31.27), the required rooftop envelope is constructed before lemma 13.19.4 is applied to the relative projection.

Moment and continuity estimates connect these operations on envelopes with existence. The compactness argument with first moments, using (10.31.10), follows [Proposition 4.2, XL26]: one chooses a reference potential in the same singularity type whose mass is sufficiently close to the upper volume, which need not be attained. Continuity for a fixed dominating measure is [Theorem 4.2, XL26]; there the finite rooftop envelopes use only the envelope class, while the two-sided bounds for the mass prevent collapse and control the tails.

The closure theorem for varying references, theorem 10.31.30, is [Corollary 4.1, XL26]. Projection to ordered lower models gives a fixed relative class for each tail of the sequence, and an exponential contact estimate prevents collapse. The stability for positive exponents in [Corollary 6.2, XL26] assumes uniformly bounded $L^ p$ data and the ordinary type of the reference. Theorem 10.31.47 treats instead the relative full-mass class: the models converge for the volume comparison with a common positive lower bound for their lower volumes, and the densities converge in $L^1$ with respect to a fixed finite non-pluripolar measure. Extracting a summable subsequence produces the dominating measure needed for the closure theorem. For a positive exponent, uniqueness gives convergence in capacity of the whole sequence of potentials. For exponent zero, the scalars and the measures converge, every $L^1$ cluster point of the normalized potentials solves the limiting equation, and the corresponding subsequence converges in capacity. In both cases, identifying the right-hand sides in $L^1$ gives convergence of the measures in total variation.

For the minimal reference, the equations with general measures in subsection 10.31.21 are [Theorems 5.2–5.3, XL26]. The estimate for higher moments in subsection 10.31.13 follows the concave-weight argument of [Proposition 5.1 and Lemma 5.1, XL26], with the integrability against the fixed singular measure stated explicitly. The smoothing of measures used in the existence proof is collected in lemma 5.44.12, lemma 5.44.10.

The conclusion of corollary 10.31.56, that for $L^ p$ data the solutions have the ordinary type of the reference, is [Corollary 6.1, XL26]. The relative estimate proposition 10.31.54 starts from a solution in the envelope class and uses a uniform moment of order $m>2n+1$. The concave-weight method is related to [Theorem 5.1, XL26], which already assumes the ordinary type of the reference and uses the moment exponent $m>n$; that theorem is not used to deduce the ordinary type of an arbitrary solution in the envelope class.

Addition of measures requires a common lower bound during truncation. The weighted construction in subsection 10.31.37 is [Proposition 6.1, XL26]. For unrestricted addition, (10.31.50) follows [Theorem 6.3, XL26]; an additional rooftop envelope gives the common lower bound needed to pass through the cutoff.

25.6 Monge–Ampère and complex Hessian equations

25.6 Normalization and adjoint measuresE1BC130DDD5C

The normalization constant can be studied through its adjoint probability measures even when the potential itself is not unique. The differential method for smooth solutions appears in Collins's work [Collins21]; theorem 11.33.4 replaces differentiation of smooth solutions by mixed products and domination.

The continuous-Hessian extension in theorem 11.34.11 uses local bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity and the finite background expansion to linearize the equation along signed potential variations. The supporting-density estimate of corollary 12.9.3 then allows Sobolev duality with lemma 11.24.1; the directional derivative is the convex-analytic identity already proved in proposition 11.34.5. The product formula in proposition 11.34.13 uses curve Green inversion and the smooth Gauduchon multiplier on the other factor. Its two-curve specialization is also covered by theorem 11.45.16 with zero divisor. The non-Dini example uses the same Hopf torsion calculation as (23.1.3), in complex dimension two.

For the mass quotient and the closed examples in section 11.42, existence and uniqueness of solutions in a prescribed singularity type are due to Darvas, Di Nezza and Lu [Theorems 1.4(i) and 4.29, pp. 2052 and 2079–2080, DDNL18mono], and the invariance of the mass under bounded changes of the potential is their [Proposition 2.1, p. 2055, DDNL18mono]. Their hypotheses are a compact Kähler manifold, a smooth closed big class, a model reference with small unbounded locus, and positive mass. The factorization with positive residual concerns the ordinary divisorial singularity types themselves; it does not assert an identity of model envelopes for every weighted sum with real coefficients.

The dictionary between toric potentials and convex functions used in section 11.43 is that of Berman and Berndtsson [arXiv v1, Sections 2.1–2.3, especially Proposition 2.3 and Lemma 2.5, pp. 10–13, BBToric13]. The angular coefficient in (11.43.4) is computed directly, in the book's conventions for the squared logarithm and the operator. The argument with finite envelopes establishes the identity for ordinary models, and a common translated simplex gives both the witness in a smaller background and the volume estimate in terms of the Hausdorff distance. The two families in subsection 11.43.9, subsection 11.43.14 satisfy these conditions explicitly; since their references have small unbounded locus, the theorem for prescribed singularity types in closed classes cited above applies. The blowup chart and the normal line of the exceptional divisor used to compute the rank and the mass of the residual are taken from [Chapter VII, equation (12.2) and Proposition 12.4, pp. 356–357, DemCADG]. These computations concern fixed modifications and closed backgrounds.

The description of the residual in proposition 11.34.18 uses the products of bounded plurisubharmonic functions of Bedford and Taylor [Section 2, BT82] and the extension of plurisubharmonic functions across pluripolar sets in [Chapter I, Theorem 5.24, DemCADG]. Integration by parts for bounded potentials against a closed positive current is established in [Theorem 1.14 and Lemma 1.15, pp. 214–217, BEGZ10]; alternatively, the cutoff in (11.34.20) can be smoothed explicitly, which makes its estimate a direct Stokes calculation for distributions. In theorem 11.34.21, the two radial profiles give the coefficients of the divisors before the limit (11.34.23) of the squares is taken. This distinguishes the relative residual adjoint from the classical adjoints of smooth potentials whose exponential densities concentrate.

For the normalization on split products in lemma 15.30.2, the smooth input is again [Corollary 1, TW10], applied to the closed projective factor. The order of the scalars for bounded densities extends the formula to continuous densities on the factor, and the original truncations determine the threshold for every smooth reference volume. The radial flux in lemma 15.30.1 and a separate calculation of non-pluripolar products then give theorem 15.30.3. The elliptic factor is the threefold of section 12.19, whose balanced metric has volume $24\pi $ by proposition 12.19.18; this gives the fivefold equation with constant $240\pi $. The bounded equation of [Theorem 0.1, KN15] and closed Stokes extend this result to every integrable density from a closed Kähler factor in theorem 15.30.6: comparison of the original truncations computes the scalar, and threshold attainment on the factor, together with its non-pluripolar mass bound, makes the lower measure an equality. The root norm formula of proposition 15.32.11 then uses the full Gauduchon test class and identifies a closed subspace of $\mathcal D_ h^0$. The radial family supplies roots outside every higher $L^ r$ class, with explicit logarithmic tails. For arbitrary densities on the product that are merely integrable and have positive threshold, the existence of an exact solution remains the problem of 24.2.2.

The same radial flux gives the criterion for exponential growth in theorem 15.35.9. Disjoint annuli in projective space and a rapidly convergent smooth baseline adapt the concentration in theorem 15.35.10 to every prescribed sequence of base densities whose scalars collapse. The bounded equations on the products determine the scalars of the components, and for every positive exponent the exponentially weighted pole absorbs their sum. The construction of greatest solutions then gives exact solutions at zero threshold, which are necessarily unbounded, in particular on the elliptic products of dimensions four and five. The explicit barriers there have masses $96\pi $ and $240\pi $, whereas the exact solutions have their own finite positive masses. A general criterion for solvability at zero threshold remains open.

That the set of solvable exponents is an upper interval, proposition 15.35.12, follows by translating a subsolution downward before increasing its exponent. For the collapse of mass at zero threshold in proposition 15.35.13, normalized exponential damping gives an $L^1$ approximation of the fixed density, and upper semicontinuity of the threshold forces the normalization scalars to tend to zero. This controls the masses of the exact solutions without identifying the limits of the normalized potentials.

The criterion for attaining a positive endpoint, proposition 15.35.16, combines the compactness of normalized potentials with the closure of subsolutions under lower bounds for the density and the existence of greatest solutions. Its common upper barrier comes from the equation of theorem 14.19.3 with the truncated, bounded density, together with singular strict domination. The corrected order in lemma 15.35.15 gives a decreasing family as the exponent decreases to a positive solvable exponent. Monotone convergence in capacity and the closedness theorem for positive exponents identify the limit from the right in proposition 15.35.17, and maximality of the greatest solutions identifies the limiting potential. Approach from below uses the regularized increasing envelope, giving the exact left limit of proposition 15.35.18. Integrating the corrected family gives a bounded increasing real function on each compact exponent interval. Its jumps detect the difference between the left limit and the greatest solution, which proves proposition 15.35.19.

For the non-$L^ p$ radial family, lemma 15.36.2 identifies the greatest solutions on the full product through the bounded factor equations and singular strict domination. The proof of theorem 15.36.5 uses their cumulative fluxes to determine the whole normalized limit, including when the density parameter varies. Local uniform convergence outside the fixed pole set and the Hermitian capacity estimate give capacity convergence on both factors and the product. No general full-mass stability theorem is needed for this radial argument. The finite or divergent first moment determines scalar centering in proposition 15.36.8. The order characterization of separated critical subsolutions in corollary 15.36.11 additionally uses Dinew's closed-class full-mass uniqueness theorem [arXiv v1, Theorem 1.2, pp. 2 and 5–8, DinewUniqueness08]; this input is applied only on the projective factor. It neither proves uniqueness of arbitrary nonclosed critical potentials nor supplies a theorem for varying singular references.

For the logarithmic product references, proposition 11.45.3 computes the ordinary envelope on the curve and identifies the product envelope by restriction to slices. Divisorial removal transfers the exponential equation and its greatestness to a bounded equation in the positive residual background, as in lemma 11.45.4. The Green operator on the curve gives uniformly bounded residuals by contraction for small exponents. Its uniformly integrable logarithmic kernel then determines the joint limit and the scalar error in theorem 11.45.9. The centering uses the critical scalar of each varying datum. The separated order characterization in corollary 11.45.13 follows from closed curve mass and the distributional equation; maximality of the coefficient in the full prescribed class follows instead from greatestness of the positive-exponent solutions. This argument uses the earlier bounded existence and domination theorems and does not impose a mass property on the Hermitian factor.

For the product surface in 11.45.14, the logarithmic model and Green residual are those of proposition 11.45.3, theorem 11.45.9. The continuous positive residual allows smooth perturbations of the singular solution, and the supporting inequality on all continuous data makes every supporting probability invariant for the weak linearization. Spherical harmonics reduce uniqueness to the signed-measure resolvent lemma lemma 11.45.15, whose proof uses the round sphere heat operator. This gives theorem 11.45.16 without an invariant-density regularity assumption. The approximation statement proposition 11.45.18 uses the already proved conformal Gauduchon theorem theorem 11.4.2 for each smooth residual; uniform tensor convergence transfers the operator and then the weighted products. The explicit pole-filling family in example 11.45.19 shows why retaining the divisor is part of this approximation statement.

The one-sided divisorial correspondence of lemma 11.41.5 extends the ordinary correspondence of theorem 11.41.1 by the nonclosed divisorial-removal lemma and locality of the extended measures. A uniform submean bound identifies the ordinary envelope type and its explicit smaller-background competitor. The whole one-sided threshold in theorem 11.41.6 then follows from theorem 15.28.4; its smooth attainment uses theorem 14.2.1, rather than a new prescribed-singularity existence theorem. Strictness follows from the elliptic cofactor identity off the divisor and the strong maximum principle. The obstruction in corollary 11.41.7 is consistent with the stronger later smooth-dual rigidity, while example 11.41.8 fixes the Fubini–Study factor to compute the precise restricted coefficient. The inverse realization problem for general densities and annihilating faces remains separate.

The curve-measure equations of section 15.31 begin with the normalized logarithmic kernel on the projective line. Its distributional curvature and the degree-one extended measure give proposition 15.31.13 by bounded product expansion and truncation. Under continuity of the potential, local Riesz decomposition gives non-polarity, while rotation smoothing and Dirichlet energy give the canonical Sobolev trace of lemma 15.31.4. The convex functional in theorem 15.31.8 yields every positive exponent; the bounded Green density and uniform logarithmic tails give continuity, and fixed barriers give uniform selection. The full-product greatestness and coefficient in theorem 15.31.15 use the earlier bounded strict domination and ordered-contact theorems. The latter retains the equality-set term when an unbounded competitor is floored by a bounded solution. The Frostman test includes nonconstant weighted circles. The zero-lower-mass conclusion assumes the factor's vanishing lower mass; the general individual-measure classification is not a consequence of this product construction.

The radial residual criterion in section 11.46 uses central mass rather than an ordinary-model envelope identity. The local decreasing-limit property gives the genuine pole, while the radial determinant flux identifies its non-pluripolar probability and inverse. The central density error controls the flux and its first derivative without differentiation of that error, giving theorem 11.46.8. Flat errors, mass-preserving sharp examples and an open zero annulus follow from the same inverse in proposition 11.46.15, proposition 11.46.17, proposition 11.46.20. The conditional nonclosed product of corollary 11.46.22 uses bounded multilinearity and pullback by a projection, as proved in proposition 5.28.2, lemma 5.28.4, followed by the actual non-pluripolar truncation limit. It assumes zero lower mass of the factor and makes no assertion about arbitrary nonsymmetric equations.

The singular-obstacle envelopes of section 11.47 use the same sublogarithmic reference as the preceding radial density criterion. Unitary invariance reduces the full envelope to a convex minorant, and supporting tangents control both ends. On the right tail, the weighted slope and second-derivative estimates in (11.47.12) give uniform projective Hessian bounds even when contact moves to infinity; interpolation with value contraction gives theorem 11.47.11. The full product formula in proposition 11.47.14 follows from exact slicing of every competitor and the bounded-product expansion before strict-superlevel truncation. It requires no mass property of the Hermitian factor. These results concern this everywhere singular obstacle and the residual in its prescribed ordinary type, while regularity for arbitrary types and compact obstacle sets remains open.

25.7 Envelopes, singularity types, and prescribed data

25.7 Envelopes and comparison3F57C7AFD15C

Narzillaev studies weighted extremal functions of a compact set $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$ with a bounded weight $\psi $ on $K$ and logarithmic growth $\delta \log ^+\lVert z\rVert $, $\delta >0$. The concavity in the growth parameter and the alternatives for regular contact in theorem 16.28.14 are stated in [v1, Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 1.1, p. 6, NarzillaevWeighted26]; the proof given here also shows directly, by scaling, that the set of parameters at which the unregularized envelope attains the obstacle on $K$ is empty or a ray. Lemma 16.28.9, Proposition 16.28.10 derive the correspondence with compact envelopes on projective space, the finiteness of the envelope and its almost-everywhere order from the compactness and extension results proved earlier in the book. In the book's convention, the growth $\delta \log ^+\lVert z\rVert $ corresponds to the projective background $(\delta /2)\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ and to the obstacle $\psi -\delta \log (1+\lVert z\rVert ^2)/2$; Narzillaev's operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /2$ is $\pi $ times the book's. None of the theorems of that preprint on products, plurithinness or weighted counterexamples is used in these proofs.

For the zero obstacle, corollary 16.28.13 gives the case of compact sets of the classical fact, recalled in [v1, Section 2, equation (4), p. 4, NarzillaevWeighted26], that removing a pluripolar set does not change the extremal function. For bounded weights, the proof uses the logarithmic pole barrier of lemma 16.28.12. Proposition 5.40.6 carries out the corresponding argument for compact sets in an arbitrary smooth big background, using the correction of pointwise competitors in lemma 5.40.5.

The estimates for increments in the growth parameter in lemma 16.28.18 are [v1, Lemma 3.1, p. 6, NarzillaevWeighted26], and at a point of regular contact proposition 16.28.20, corollary 16.28.24 recover [v1, Proposition 3.2, p. 7, NarzillaevWeighted26]. The proof given here keeps the estimates for the initial and the later slopes at every point of $\mathbb C^ n$ and every positive growth parameter, including the uniform error for large increments. The representation by probability measures and the attained derivative in theorem 16.28.27, theorem 16.28.29 come from [v1, Theorems 3.3–3.4, pp. 8–9, NarzillaevWeighted26]; the same argument with the finite envelope extends them to every point and every positive parameter. The passage to weak limits of these probability measures uses the continuity of the weight. The joint response to changes of the weight and of the growth, and the criteria for differentiability, in lemma 16.28.33, proposition 16.28.35, corollary 16.28.37, corollary 16.28.39, follow directly from the attained representation and the compactness of its set of active pairs. Example 16.28.40 gives an explicit corner in the dependence on the weight, on the closed unit disk.

The relative extremal function of definition 5.27.4 follows the convention for compact sets in [v1, Section 2, equation (8), p. 5, NarzillaevWeighted26]. Lemma 16.28.43, which shows that the relative extremal function equals $-1$ at a point exactly when the global extremal function vanishes there, is proved by an explicit logarithmic gluing and the pole barrier above. Lemma 16.28.45, Theorem 16.28.46 give [v1, Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.2, p. 10, NarzillaevWeighted26], including the local strictness hypothesis $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi \geq c\omega _0$ near the point, with $\omega _0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\lVert z\rVert ^2$, a global weight $\Psi $ in the given growth class extending the weight on $K$, and the closed compact pieces inside the ball. Narzillaev's operator and Euclidean form are both $\pi $ times those of the book, so the coefficient $c$ and the bound for the defect are unchanged. The pointwise consequence for the Hessian in corollary 16.28.48 is the observation following that theorem on p. 10.

The planar disks and the quantitative barrier of lemma 16.28.50 come from [v1, Lemma 6.1, pp. 12–13, NarzillaevWeighted26]. Proposition 16.28.51 proves part of the product construction in [v1, Lemma 6.2, pp. 13–14, NarzillaevWeighted26], namely the contact defect along the exceptional fiber and the failure of plurithinness at the interior point specified there. The logarithmic series is constructed by convergence of canonical representatives on compact sets, and an explicit pole barrier produces competitors that satisfy the obstacle everywhere. The proof needs neither a general product formula nor a classification at all boundary points.

The formula on normal fibers for the pluricomplex Green function with a divisorial pole, proposition 5.40.10, is the case of the unit ball of Dao, Nguyen and Tran's [v1, Proposition 4.2, p. 25, DNTGreen26], with logarithms normalized as $\log |\zeta |^2$ in the normal coordinate $\zeta $; the proof uses the maximum principle in one variable. The bounded minorants of proposition 5.40.12 converge at every interior point, including the points of the divisor, with an explicit error bound. This is a special model for the approximation by bounded envelopes in [Theorem 1.7, pp. 5–6, DNTGreen26], whose general result assumes an inward deformation in a sector and uses B-regularity for continuity. The calculation of boundary cluster values in example 5.40.15 concerns the trace of the divisor on the boundary, whereas that theorem asserts continuity inside the domain.

Contact sets connect the order of potentials with the order of their Monge–Ampère measures. For semipositive big backgrounds, theorem 16.28.5 is due to Alehyane, Lu and Salouf [Theorem 2.2, ALS26]; the passage from bounded to unbounded potentials in the book removes the bigness assumption and a uniform mass assumption. For a general big background, Boucksom, Guedj and Lu [Theorem 2.9 and Proposition 2.11, BGL25] prove that the measure of the envelope is concentrated on the contact set under bounded mass, and local replacement together with a strict singular barrier gives theorem 15.8.6 without that assumption.

The measure estimate for envelope fixed points, proposition 16.28.7, is [Proposition 2.12, ALS26]. Let $\theta $ be smooth and semipositive, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $ for the ordinary envelope of definition 5.40.4. The proof given here uses the identity $P_\theta (\varphi +1,0)=\varphi $, where $P_\theta (\varphi +1,0)$ is the largest $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function lying below $\min (\varphi +1,0)$ (section 5.40); contact with the first obstacle occurs only on the pluripolar set $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $, so only contact with zero contributes to the measure. For bounded potentials, the proof of the domination principle by envelopes, theorem 16.28.56, is due to Guedj and Lu [Proposition 2.8, GL22].

Difference envelopes give a relative class in which singular potentials can still be compared. The construction appears for semipositive big backgrounds in [Proposition 2.4 and Lemma 2.5, ALS26] and for arbitrary big backgrounds in Xuan Li's [Section 2.1, XL26]; the estimate for sublevel sets shows that the envelope is not identically $-\infty $ as soon as its family of competitors is nonempty. The relative envelope class of definition 16.28.61 follows [Definition 3.2, ALS26], and the proof of its closure under convex stretching, lemma 16.28.63, is the argument of [Proposition 3.5, ALS26].
