The condition (16.28.67) on the reference and its consequence, positivity of the mass of each individual potential in the class, appear in [Proposition 2.10 and the discussion after Definition 2.13, ALS26]; that paper does not assume bounded mass for its equations with $L^ p$ data in a fixed ordinary type. This positivity for individual potentials must be distinguished from a positive infimum of the mass over the whole ordinary singularity type. The mechanism giving the lower bound for the mass in theorem 16.28.70 is that of [Proposition 3.8, ALS26].

For lower semicontinuous obstacles the contact argument requires an approximation. The proof of proposition 16.28.3 follows Guedj and Lu [Theorem 2.3, GL22] and uses the Bedford–Taylor convergence theorem for increasing bounded sequences [Theorem 7.4, BT82]; smooth local corrections and an expansion against the remaining background extend it to nonclosed backgrounds.

The modified comparison principle, theorem 14.19.6, is due to Kołodziej and Nguyen [Theorem 0.2, KN15]. The proof given here follows the finite induction of Guedj and Lu [Theorem 1.5, GL22], with larger dimensional constants.

25.8 Energy, geodesics, rays, and metric geometry

25.8 Closed classes and metric completeness889877FC2044

The examples theorem 10.24.1, theorem 10.24.7, theorem 10.24.16 test the completeness question raised by Di Nezza, Guedj and Lu [v1, Theorem 3.4 and Question 3.5, pp. 14–15, DNGL26]. The first uses a big class that is not nef and an ordinary solution with minimal singularities. The second has a semipositive nef and big background, a solution of full mass and finite energy with vanishing Lelong numbers, and the prescribed nonintegrable pole with smooth strictly positive coefficient; its cusp is complete, but a disjoint null curve lies at finite normal distance. The third, theorem 10.24.16, satisfies exactly the identities of [v1, Section 3.1, pp. 12–14, DNGL26] for the initial potential, the resolution, the discrepancy, the class and the prescribed volume. Its class is not nef and has a divisorial reference with minimal singularities, while the solution adds a cusp with vanishing Lelong numbers along a disjoint curve. These examples disprove the two separate completeness assertions for the elliptic equations; whether nefness and compatibility can hold simultaneously, and whether the evolving maximal flow itself is complete, remain open. The torus examples for normal lengths in section 10.25 have instead logarithmically weakened poles whose coefficients tend to zero at the divisor.

The energy argument in section 10.24 uses the classical finite-energy class of [Section 2, BEGZ10], relative to a reference with minimal singularities; finiteness of the mixed masses and of the relative energy comes from [Proposition 1.6 and Section 2.2, BEGZ10]. Uniqueness follows from the comparison principle for full mass [Corollary 2.3, BEGZ10]: the unweighted reference measure is infinite, but the two Monge–Ampère measures being compared are finite.

In subsection 10.24.6, the potential with minimal singularities is $V_\theta =0$, and exact radial identities show that the volume form is smooth and positive across both divisors. The bounded truncations have masses $1-p(T_ k)^2$ for the square and $1-p(T_ k)$ for the mixed product on the transition shell, where $p$ is the slope of the radial profile and $T_ k$ the radius at which the truncation at level $k$ begins; their contributions to the energy tend to zero. The products are computed by smooth convex approximation and the continuity along decreasing sequences proved by Bedford and Taylor [Theorem 2.1, pp. 4–7, BT82]. This direct computation of the energy agrees with the criterion by canonical approximation of [Propositions 2.10–2.11, arXiv pp. 26–27, BEGZ10]. Here vanishing Lelong numbers do not imply ordinary minimal singularities.

In subsection 10.24.13, radial barriers and the inversion of a Volterra operator construct the cusp along the curve for a fixed smooth volume form, and explicit charts on the blowup give a smooth positive residual volume and a Kähler residual at the initial time. The reference with minimal singularities is obtained from the extension across isolated points in lemma 5.24.8. The canonical truncations at level $k$ have cutoff energy $O(k\mathrm{e}^{-k/2})$, so the continuity of bounded products and the criteria for relative energy cited above apply. The remaining smooth pulled-back metric puts the exceptional curve at finite distance. This is an auxiliary solution of an elliptic equation; it is not identified with the evolving smoothing metric.

Hölder regularity imposes a further restriction on the metric. If a positive residual current has a Hölder continuous potential and is smooth and strictly positive outside a proper analytic set, theorem 5.39.1 shows that every point of that set lies at finite distance in the metric completion; on a compact manifold, removing a nonempty analytic set therefore gives an incomplete metric. Continuity alone allows complete ends: for the prescribed radial densities of theorem 10.22.7, boundedness of the minimal remainder and finiteness of the normal length have different logarithmic thresholds. The resulting complete examples with bounded potentials solve equations with prescribed densities; they do not have the compatibility with the flow discussed above.

The mechanism of Dang [v2, Proposition 5.2, pp. 16–17, Dang26], which bounds distances through a Dini condition on the square root of the modulus of continuity of the potential, is the subject of theorem 5.39.6. The trace calculation given here keeps the smooth background through the additive term in (5.39.5) and needs no doubling condition. It gives logarithmic rates and uniform limits of pseudometrics along subsequences in corollary 5.39.7, corollary 5.39.8; a common positive lower bound for the metrics is needed to exclude collapse.

25.9 Sections, convex bodies, and non-Archimedean geometry

25.9 Section growth and partial kernels482A6169B3A6

The growth of sections links singular potentials to the algebraic dimension through a projective modification. The form of Moishezon's theorem used in section 19.9 is stated in [Introduction, p. 1332, Moi67]; it is used as a classical geometric input. A Kähler modification also gives the bounded mass conclusion of lemma 19.9.12, by Guedj and Lu's argument pulling back upper volumes [Lemma 3.6, GL22].

For section rings constructed through the algebraic reduction, see Xiaojun Wu's [Wu24]. The flag construction in section 19.9 uses a fixed compact flag on an auxiliary modification; it makes no assertion about the centers of arbitrary valuations of the field of meromorphic functions.

The maximum at maximal mapping rank in proposition 19.9.19 is Qin's [v1, Proposition B.1, pp. 35–36, QinCurvatureRank26]. The scalar and flag bounds in corollary 19.9.20 use the section-ratio field and period count already established in this book, with the curvature rank measured on its semipositive locus. The fixed-twist and endpoint deductions, Euler polynomial, surface estimate and sharp product follow [v1, Sections 10.2–10.3 and Example 11.1, pp. 32–34, QinCurvatureRank26]; they are independent of that paper's all-degree finite-jet estimate, Theorem A.

Principalization and its isomorphism off the base ideal are Włodarczyk's [Theorem 2.0.3, p. 35, and Lemma 4.0.3, p. 42, Wlo09]. The image dimension, proper mapping and Chow inputs are given with proofs in [Chapter II, Corollary 8.6, Theorem 8.8 and Theorem 8.10, pp. 118–121, DemCADG]. Serre duality uses the compact Hermitian setting of [Chapter VI, Theorem 7.3, p. 310, DemCADG]. The analytic Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch formula used in proposition 19.9.23 is [Theorem (3.4), p. 163, Ati64]; it applies to compact complex manifolds and requires no Kähler hypothesis.

The formulas for derivatives in the weight and the Gevrey bounds in proposition 18.34.5, theorem 18.34.6, corollary 18.34.9 follow the mechanism for bounded weights of Marinescu and Xing [v1, Theorems 1.1–1.2, pp. 2–3, and Section 3, pp. 11–19, MarinescuXingParameter26], applied to the fixed space of selected sections on a compact manifold. The proof uses the inverse of a compressed Gram matrix and its finite jets, while the degree and the multiplier-ideal space stay fixed. The example example 18.34.12, concerning control at the boundary, is the explicit example on the disk on p. 3 of that preprint. Marinescu and Xing point to the earlier theory of bounded perturbations of Pasternak-Winiarski; its theorems involving the distance to the boundary require additional weighted openness estimates and are not used in these compact arguments.

The estimates for the probability measures in lemma 18.34.16, proposition 18.34.18, proposition 18.34.22 follow directly from the reproducing identities in finite dimension. Positivity of the symmetric coupling defined by the squared kernel gives the factor one half in the bound for infinitesimal variations, and integrating the logarithm of the odds of the probability of each Borel set gives a sharper modulus for the global oscillation; the smooth example of rank one, example 18.34.21, shows that this modulus is optimal as a supremum. Normalizing by the dimension gives a uniform radius of analyticity after rescaling. The calculation on a product in example 18.34.24 expresses the conditional fiber probabilities of section 18.40 as a perturbation of the norm weight of order inverse to the degree. Its nonzero limit of intrinsic measures and its unchanged limit of logarithmic potentials describe different parts of the kernel data.

In the fiber-integrability criterion of theorem 18.39.8, corollary 18.39.9, example 18.39.10, a radial calculation on a simplex detects the strict endpoint of integrability and the weighted gain $p\sum _ jb_ j^{-1}$, where $p$ and $b_ j$ are the exponents of the normal and the fiber variables in the anisotropic model of the selecting potential. A global lower bound and a single chart with an upper bound then give a bounded divisorial band, whose loss of sections is controlled by the dimension estimate lemma 18.39.1. This extends the isotropic theorem on sections vanishing along a divisor, without claiming that the condition is necessary for arbitrary selecting potentials.

Theorem 18.39.13 extends this argument to finite families of divisors with simple normal crossings. The calculation of the ideal on the base uses separated normal coordinates, and lemma 18.39.12 controls all the mixed twists arising in the restrictions. In the product model of example 18.39.14, integrability at points where several poles meet is established directly, by Fubini's theorem in distinct pairs of base and fiber coordinates.

The criterion on a modified base, theorem 18.39.16, combines the same argument with the transformation rule for adjoint ideals, lemma 5.43.22, and the pushforward identity for non-pluripolar products, proposition 18.35.1. The projective model with a point pole in example 18.39.17 makes explicit the Jacobian order $q-1$, where $q$ is the dimension of the base, and the positive residual on the blowup. The criterion assumes that the modification and its divisorial data are given; it does not assert that they exist for an arbitrary selecting potential.

Corollary 18.39.19 separates the curvature requirements in these proofs: a smooth semipositive residual gives a positive reference current, and a positive top-degree integral gives it the required mass, while the estimates for integrability and restriction need no strict positivity of the curvature. In example 18.39.20 the original base is a blowup. Its contracted lines prevent any choice of gauge from making the residual strictly positive, while Hartogs extension shows that, because of the fixed exceptional divisor, the selected space and the reference space coincide.

The calculation of coefficients in proposition 18.39.22 combines this Hartogs identification with the anisotropic local threshold; the remaining conditions are ordinary jet conditions at points of projective space. Exact counts of homogeneous monomials then identify the range of the references in which the mass is positive, the drop in degree at the boundary of this range, and the tensor power at which a more singular selecting potential removes every section.

The model with two points in example 18.39.25 keeps positive top-degree volume while the residual has degree zero on the curve joining the two centers. Its nonzero defect, of degree $q-1$, is computed by lemma 18.39.24, which constructs simultaneous jets from affine linear factors and finite Taylor division and requires the sum of the jet orders to be at most the projective degree plus one. Thus a sharp loss of sections and the obstruction to a smooth strictly positive residual occur in the same explicit family.

The metric on projective space in section 18.43 is the one in Chiang's [v1, Example I.15, pp. 9–10, ChiangKernel26]. The proof of proposition 18.43.3 computes the global norms of monomials directly, in the convention $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm e^{-\phi }$ for a local frame $e$ with weight $\phi $, and for a given integration volume; it uses neither the general spectral localization theorem nor the chain of expansions by Newton polyhedra of that preprint. The transition for growing jets on a compact curve, theorem 18.42.1, is the result obtained by comparison with a disk in the preceding section on curves, and its full extension to all sublinear orders, at the boundary of the region where the curvature vanishes, is theorem 18.42.15.

The correction on shrinking scales in lemma 18.42.13 uses the $L^2$ estimate with pointwise inverse curvature of [Theorem 5.2 and its singular-metric extension, pp. 34–35, DemAM11], whose Hilbert-space estimate comes from the preceding Theorem 5.1 and its proof on pp. 33–34. Applying the estimate to $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$, where $L$ is the line bundle on the compact curve $C$ and $K_ C$ is the canonical bundle of $C$, takes the Ricci curvature into account, and a bounded function varying on the scale $R$ of the flat region restores strictly positive curvature inside it. The particular free boundary in lemma 18.42.10 is constructed by solving an equation for Fourier coefficients in fixed Hölder spaces of finite order and applying the implicit function theorem in Banach spaces. The argument with Gaussian annuli then gives theorem 18.42.15, theorem 18.42.27 directly, including slowly growing orders, uniformity in the angle, sharpness on compact curves and the limitation of finite Taylor corrections.

On the explicit compact product in section 18.44, global orthogonal monomials turn ordinary jet conditions of total order into a selection by a half-space. The transition for one curve factor gives the marginal Gaussian laws used in theorem 18.44.2, and the calculation of moments at a fixed positive radius, together with the exact trace, gives convergence in total variation. The sharp radial correction in proposition 18.44.8 follows from the positive first remainder assumed there. Theorem 18.44.11 then uses the integrability calculation at an isolated pole and constancy along compact connected fibers to transfer norms and kernels exactly; the normalization on the base and the matching of volumes are part of its statement.

The selection by an interior Newton polytope in section 18.45 is set up with an integral affine offset, a polytope in the interior, a strictly convex invariant logarithmic weight and a positive invariant sampling probability on the whole compact manifold. Angular orthogonality gives exact norms, lattice approximation gives the lower bound for the envelope, and uniform concentration gives the shell measure in the relative dimension. The local argument with Hessian minors distinguishes this measure from mixed non-pluripolar curvature in lower dimension. The construction does not identify an arbitrary multiplier-ideal envelope.

The critical product of multiplier ideals in section 18.46 is computed directly from the integrability formula for smooth centers and the identity for an atom in the plane. Exhausting the curvature mass fiber by fiber identifies its multiplier-ideal envelope. Exact norms given by beta integrals, together with concentration, give two kernel limits depending on parity, whereas dividing by the exact dimension gives a single limit of probability measures. The calculation shows that a fixed growth exponent does not imply convergence of the leading coefficient in the count of sections, even when the growth dimension is positive.

For the selection by multiplier ideals at the base points of a pencil in section 18.47, the lower bound for Lelong numbers implied by inclusions of multiplier ideals at all weights, together with a radial convex maximum, identifies the full classes of competitors for both the multiplier-ideal and the ordinary envelopes, and restriction to the curves of degree two in the pencil controls the competitors that are not invariant. Exact norms of truncated Gaussians keep track of the three bands of finite degree, whose count gives the limiting intrinsic mass three. The bounds at the poles also give convergence in every finite $L^ p$ and uniform convergence of the exponentials, while excluding a uniform additive error on the whole manifold. The compact sampling box and the obstacle are part of the statement.

25.10 Singular spaces, traces, and locally conformally Kähler geometry

25.10 Perron geometry on Hopf manifoldsF14EBE94C297

The closed-base metric inputs in subsection 17.16.15 are Darvas' Kähler completion and CAT$(0)$ theorems [v3, Theorems 6.1 and 9.2, pp. 20–26 and 30–32, DarvasCompletion17]. Capacity endpoint attainment and preservation of the squared-energy class are [v3, Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.4, pp. 18–20, DarvasCompletion17]. The full-mass model characterization used in proposition 17.16.32 is [v3, Theorem 4.3, pp. 16–17, DarvasCompletion17]. These theorems are applied on the connected compact Kähler base $\mathbb P^{n-1}$. The source uses $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $, so potentials are divided by $2\pi $ in (17.16.21); fiber integration contributes the additional factor $\sqrt{2n}$ to distance.

The smooth-endpoint distance formula used in proposition 17.16.22, proposition 17.16.29 is [v3, equation (15), p. 8, and Theorem 7.2, p. 28, DarvasCompletion17]. The bounded Dirichlet description is [v3, Section 2.2, equations (16)–(17), p. 9, DarvasCompletion17]. Section 7, p. 27, gives a bounded-potential counterexample to using the initial-velocity formula outside its regularity hypotheses. The completed action in the book is therefore defined by metric speed.

The Hopf conclusions use the elliptic fiber action and the bounded products with smooth corrections already established in the book, followed by canonical finite-level truncation. No bounded-mass property of the Hopf manifold is imposed. Group averaging proves stationarity under all smooth variations, and radial Fourier modes give the negative raw-action directions in theorem 17.16.25. The explicit diagonal geodesics and singular radial family supply exact distance and energy calculations. Their metric is on basic potentials; its ordinary-model projection is zero throughout the finite-energy domain, so it does not solve the general ordinary-model metric problem.

25.10 Singular spaces, traces, and locally conformally Kähler geometry

25.10 Locally conformally Kähler geometryF14EBE94C297

In locally conformally Kähler geometry, the Lee form constrains both the rigidity of metrics and the volume forms that can be prescribed. The conjecture on pseudoeffectivity of the Lee class, 23.2.12, is formulated in terms of Gauduchon degrees by Ornea and Verbitsky [arXiv version, Conjecture 4.14 and Remark 4.16, OV25Balanced]; its consequence for balanced metrics is proposition 23.2.11. Their theorem on the volume forms of Vaisman metrics [arXiv version, Theorem 4.1 and Lemmas 4.2–4.4, OV24Vaisman] requires invariance under both the Lee and the anti-Lee vector fields. The proof of theorem 23.2.29 uses theorem 14.2.1: uniqueness gives a basic potential, transverse integration by Stokes' theorem fixes the scalar, and the Lee form of the new metric is parallel because it is closed and its dual vector field is Killing. The uniqueness argument keeps the scale of the candidate metric in (23.2.34) as an unknown until integration determines it.

The least-eigenvalue criterion 23.2.15 is proved by applying smooth Stokes to the volume polynomial of 23.2.14. Nonvanishing of the ordinary Bott–Chern class already follows from the conformal Gauduchon argument and the Lee degree (23.2.8). The Hopf calculations in 23.2.16, 23.2.17 distinguish constancy of the least eigenvalue from constancy of the whole spectrum, and distinguish first pointwise degeneration from collapse of total volume. These are explicit compact metrics in every dimension at least two. The criterion gives a smooth semipositive representative under its spectral hypothesis; pseudoeffectivity without that hypothesis remains the conjecture above.

The classification of radial metrics in 23.2.35 follows from explicit identities for the Hopf forms and a periodic scalar equation. Its positive periodic solutions are strictly ordered by the constant of integration, and their Lee periods fill the negative half-line. The positive twisted potential is constructed in the gauge given by the Lee form of the metric itself. Nonconstant radial volume forms force the metric to be non-Vaisman, and uniqueness of the metric is asserted only within the radial family considered there.

The proof of theorem 23.2.47 keeps the divergence terms in the Chern–Ricci-flat specialization of the argument of Barbaro and Otiman [v2, Section 4, equations (2)–(4), pp. 12–13, BO25LCK]. Their Theorem A gives the Gauduchon rigidity conclusion; retaining the scalar-curvature term in the integrated Bianchi identity gives the divergence identity and the equivalence with holomorphicity of the Lee field. The quotient and the two metrics in example 23.2.53 are computed directly: the holomorphic volume trivializes the canonical bundle, the flat gauge has nonzero Lee divergence, and compact pluriharmonic rigidity prevents a simultaneous conformal gauge. The conjecture for manifolds, 23.2.54, is stated in [Introduction, BO25LCK]. The Kodaira example admits a Vaisman metric on its given complex structure, so its conformal obstruction does not refute that conjecture.

The dual description of the Lee–Gauduchon cone and its bimeromorphic invariance in subsection 23.2.55 are due to Ornea and Verbitsky [Theorems 3.11 and 4.5, OV25LeeGauduchon]. The distinction between vanishing of the Lee–Gauduchon class and the strongly Gauduchon condition in subsection 23.2.67 follows [Remarks 5.6–5.8, OV25LeeGauduchon], and the criterion for the existence of strongly Gauduchon metrics used there is due to Popovici [Proposition 1.2, Pop13SG].

25.10 Singular spaces, traces, and locally conformally Kähler geometry

25.10 Regularity and singular spacesF14EBE94C297

Regularity in a big class is first a local question on the locus where strict barriers are smooth. For a closed class on a compact Kähler manifold, existence and uniqueness for (10.20.2) are due to Boucksom, Eyssidieux, Guedj and Zeriahi [Theorem A, equivalently Theorem 3.1, BEGZ10], and the bounds (10.20.3) in terms of minimal singularities are [Theorem B, quantitatively Theorem 4.1, BEGZ10]. The same uniqueness theorem for full mass identifies the solutions in closed classes in section 15.22, section 15.23, section 10.22, section 10.23. Smoothness on the ample locus in the nef case is [Theorem C, BEGZ10]; theorem 10.20.1 gives this smoothness in every closed big class, for a smooth positive volume form.

For a big background that need not be closed, the local Hölder theorem theorem 15.17.1 is Dang's [v1, Theorem A and Theorem 3.1, Dang26]. It gives the local input for the argument on the ample locus, while allowing the global potential to be unbounded and the lower curvature bound to be nonclosed. Formulating the equation with a positive scalar and only on the regular locus is equivalent, since the complementary analytic set carries neither smooth volume nor non-pluripolar mass.

The proof of local regularity also needs a quantitative stability estimate. The estimate with a strict barrier in section 15.15 is [v1, Theorem 3.3 and Remark 3.4, Dang26] in the case of minimal singularities, with the comparison potential normalized explicitly; the construction with auxiliary subsolutions in section 15.4 first treats a semipositive big background.

The interior regularity theorem theorem 15.18.1 combines this Hölder control with the assumption that the density is smooth and positive on the whole regular locus of one fixed strict analytic barrier. This domain is part of the hypothesis: smoothness of the density on a smaller open set does not give the same conclusion by restriction. The compact Pogorelov example example 10.21.10 has a smooth positive density on an inner chart, but its density loses regularity along the divisor in the gluing region, so it does not satisfy this hypothesis.

Local smoothing uses the theorem of Guan and Li on the Dirichlet problem [Theorem 1.1, p. 1186, GL10]. In (15.21.3) the background is zero and, in local coordinates $z$, the metric is $(\mathrm i/2)\partial \bar\partial |z|^2$; for a smooth positive density $G$, a large quadratic correction gives a strict subsolution. The same theorem constructs the approximants in subsection 15.18.7 and starts the passage to continuous boundary values and to zero density in section 15.7; in dimension one it is replaced by the Dirichlet problem for the Poisson equation. Once (15.18.6) is uniformly elliptic, the Evans–Krylov theorem for variable coefficients [Definition 3.2, Theorem 3.4, and the paragraph following it, TWWY15], followed by difference quotients and Schauder estimates, gives smoothness.

The local identification in section 15.21 uses Bedford and Taylor's uniqueness theorem for the bounded Dirichlet problem [Corollary 4.4, p. 17, BT82]. Degeneration of the density also matters for global stability: Kołodziej and Nguyen [Theorem 4.1, KN21] assume that the density satisfies $f\geq c_0$ for a constant $c_0>0$, in addition to their hypotheses on capacity. The densities giving nonuniqueness in section 14.20 have no such lower bound, even when they are positive almost everywhere.

For compact sets in a Hermitian manifold, Ahn [Theorems 1.1–1.2, Ahn26] proves that Hölder continuity of the extremal function is a pointwise local property. The weighted version assumes that both the unweighted extremal function and the weight are Hölder continuous, and that the set is uniformly dense in capacity; the same density condition enters the equivalence with the local and weakly local Hölder properties. These are the regularity settings referred to in section 24.1.

On singular spaces, regularity on a resolution must be combined with descent. Dang [v1, Theorem B, Dang26] proves continuity results for bounded solutions on resolutions under additional geometric and integrability hypotheses, notably for log terminal singularities; this result does not cover the arbitrary unibranch singularities in the problem posed in section 24.1. Pan [Theorems A and A', Pan25] constructs a Gauduchon metric on the regular locus of a compact reduced irreducible Hermitian space of dimension at least two; it is conformal and uniformly comparable to the given metric, and unique up to scale among such metrics. Control of the conformal factors on a resolution is central to the construction. This result motivates the questions about singular traces in section 24.1.

The boundary-weighted quadric surface in 9.11.10 is Seo's [v1, Example 6.2, pp. 29–30, SeoToricIdeals26]. The paper uses the weight $\mathrm{e}^{-2\varphi }$, so the potential here is $u=2\varphi $. The adapted volume comes from a generator of $\omega _ X^{[4]}(4D)$ and pulls back to a constant times $|s|^{-1}$ times Euclidean volume on the finite quotient cover. Splitting the logarithmic quadrant gives the strict monomial test; angular orthogonality and division of convergent series give the full ideal. This proves the explicit example directly, without using the paper's general Newton-body description. The boundary-weighted ideal and the resolution-ideal relation in proposition 9.11.9 use different volume conventions.

The affine toric monomial test in theorem 9.11.20 is the holomorphic-character part of Seo's [v1, Theorem 6.1, pp. 28–29, SeoToricIdeals26], here restricted to full-dimensional cones and effective rational boundary. Its convex-cone criterion is [v1, Lemma 4.4 and Theorem 4.6, pp. 18–19, SeoToricIdeals26]; the proof here obtains coercivity by a compactness argument and sandwiches the actual logarithmic neighborhoods between translated cones. The subtraction test of corollary 9.11.22 is the integral calculation behind [v1, Proposition 5.10 and Corollary 6.3, pp. 27 and 30, SeoToricIdeals26]. For this holomorphic-character integrability assertion the exponent can be any positive real number, without assigning a rational boundary to the subtracted weight. The quadric threefold and its whole-germ ideal in proposition 9.11.23 are computed directly from the same criterion and the homogeneous coordinate ring. No general fractional-sheaf generation or ideal-envelope statement is used.

In the construction on unibranch curves in subsection 9.11.50, the Green function, the exact mass of the pole, uniqueness in the full singularity type, descent through disks and the projective cusp are all obtained directly. $L^ p$ data on the normalization, $p>1$, give a continuous residual even when the background coming from a local embedding pulls back to a degenerate form. The example of the cusp also computes the exact threshold for densities on the singular curve. This is a result in dimension one; it neither extends the theorem on log terminal singularities cited above nor gives a general equation on nonclosed singular spaces.

The calculation at the endpoint in theorem 9.11.60 is another direct construction from the Green function of the curve and the radial primitive of theorem 10.23.1. For one logarithmic family it distinguishes three properties: finite mass of the density, a bounded residual in the ordinary singularity type, and equivalence of multiplier ideals at all weights. It does not characterize arbitrary integrable data.

The equations with nonclosed backgrounds on products with cuspidal curves in subsection 9.11.63 combine a correction of the reference to a smooth positive form, quantitative Fourier inversion, and a comparison of bounded energies in a background all of whose powers are $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. The weighted limit lemma 5.27.2 is proved by adding one complex variable $w$ and passing to the maxima with $\log |w|^2$, which reduces it to the ordinary convergence of mixed products along decreasing sequences, including top-degree products in one higher dimension. The corresponding classical input is Bedford and Taylor's [Theorem 2.4 and its proof, pp. 7–9, BT82]; their operator is $4\pi $ times ours, so products of degree $r$ scale by $(4\pi )^{-r}$. The resulting family with small data in all variables has Hölder continuous solutions on the ambient space, unique among all bounded competitors. The existence of bounded solutions for arbitrary nonnegative $L^ p$ data on the normalization, $p>1$, follows separately from theorem 10.31.3. These results complement the construction with Green functions on curves, without giving a general equation on singular spaces or a sharp criterion for densities on the singular space.

25.10 Singular spaces, traces, and locally conformally Kähler geometry

25.10 Singularity classes and tracesF14EBE94C297

The countable-pole construction of theorem 18.13.1 uses the local decreasing-limit and canonical-representative theorems in Demailly's book [Chapter I, Theorems 5.4 and 5.8, pp. 39–40, DemCADG]. Its exponential integrability follows directly from weighted Jensen's inequality and the sublinear logarithmic profiles. The envelope argument of proposition 18.13.4 uses Choquet's lemma and the local upper-envelope theorem [Chapter I, Lemma 4.23 and Theorem 5.7, pp. 38–40, DemCADG], through the exact nonclosed-background construction of section 5.40. The bounded unrestricted envelope has the same trivial multiplier ideals as the constructed potential, so it is a competitor for the ideal-equivalence envelope used here. The fixed stronger potential supplies ordinary competitors below every continuous obstacle; the general zero-obstacle implication remains open.

A theory of singularities for nonclosed backgrounds must record torsion as well as divisorial information. The quotient of the space of smooth real $(1,1)$-forms by the forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, $f$ smooth, used in section 10.30, appears in [Section 1, BGL25]; fixing the exterior derivative of the form keeps this datum on each modification.

Resolution makes additivity of traces accessible to approximation by multiplier ideals. The comparison in theorem 20.3.4 is the argument underlying Cao's additivity theorem [proof of Theorem 1.4, Cao15], and it does not require a closed global background. The recovery theorem theorem 13.21.7 combines the arguments with decreasing models and stretching with the local criterion for multiplier ideals. Uniform exponential integrability bounds each local divisorial order of the auxiliary potentials, so the proof does not require a local modification to extend over the compact manifold. The construction on a ruled surface in subsection 16.29.15, based on Demailly, Peternell and Schneider's [Example 1.7, DPS94], exhibits the boundary behavior relevant to this recovery.

The transverse recovery of theorem 16.29.22 uses the same positive-volume theorem on $\mathbb P^2$, while the Hopf threefold itself has unbounded upper mass by theorem 23.1.1. The full ideal envelope is invariant under the elliptic action because its complete competitor family is invariant; a horizontal current test then identifies it with the base envelope. The nonanalytic family uses the summable divisorial criterion of 13.24.8, whose closed mass and valuative inputs are described above. The general exact-pullback identities in proposition 16.28.59, proposition 18.4.3 follow from the descent, ideal transform and non-pluripolar product foundations; they do not assert recovery over arbitrary new Hermitian perturbations on a modified manifold.

The continuity of model envelopes in closed classes used in theorem 20.3.33 is due to Darvas and Xia [Proposition 2.1, DX24]; it is also presented in [Proposition 3.1.12, SGPT]. The argument for Lelong numbers uses small convex corrections from Darvas, Di Nezza and Lu [Lemma 4.3, DDNL21]. It suffices to apply this continuity on the submanifold, because the restricted approximants have a common curvature bound even when the ambient background is not closed.

The projective-base construction of subsection 20.3.41 uses the same positive-mass convergence of decreasing closed models; the October 4, 2026 version of the lecture manuscript gives the statement and proof in [Proposition 3.1.12, pp. 96–97, with Lemma 2.4.4, pp. 67–71, SGPT26Oct]. The ideal-class argument uses its compact Kähler criterion [Proposition 3.2.1, pp. 122–123, SGPT26Oct]; the cofinality discussion on p. 497 covers prime divisors on arbitrary compact smooth models by finite smooth blowup models. These are closed-base inputs. The finite extraction proof in lemma 20.3.44 uses proper mapping for analytic sets and analytic resolution which preserves the whole nonsingular locus, in the form of Włodarczyk's [Theorem 2.0.1(1), p. 34, Wlo09]. Its ramification argument uses the local Siu decomposition and Skoda integrability recalled in the foundations. Elliptic symmetry gives the full Hopf envelope and its mass and approximation formulas; the ideal-class argument remains on the projective base.

The residual condition in (18.27.1) implies vanishing of point Lelong numbers by scaling the uniform Lelong bound, and vanishing of polar curvature by the Gauduchon trace and bounded-type invariance. The argument persists on every smooth compact modification. The ideal neutrality of lemma 5.37.5 combines Bergman approximation and the local ideal-addition calculus; the needed Bergman estimate and strong openness are stated in [v2, Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 2.3, DemCohomology15]. The smoothing step in lemma 18.27.3 is Demailly's [Main Theorem 1.1 and Section 2, Dem92], applied to the closed current $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q'$ with smooth representative zero and lower bound $\epsilon h-B$. In the source normalization the potential is $q'/2$. The curvature of a fixed tangent metric is bounded by a large multiple of $h$, and its continuous Lelong approximants converge uniformly to zero. Richberg smoothing is applied to the continuous attenuation intermediates. This operation supplies a smooth positive residual background; the prescribed ordinary type is recovered with an actual small-curvature representative in theorem 18.27.4. The normal crossing ideal formula in proposition 20.3.8 uses ambient ideals and therefore remains meaningful when the naive residual restriction has poles everywhere on the target.

The full ordinary-type optimization in theorem 20.3.66 uses the closed comparison theorem of Boucksom, Eyssidieux, Guedj and Zeriahi [Theorem 1.16, pp. 217–218, BEGZ10] in both orders, in degrees one and two. Their Definition 1.2, p. 204, applies because every residual potential is locally bounded outside the divisor. Finiteness and closedness of the auxiliary non-pluripolar products are their [Proposition 1.6 and Theorem 1.8, pp. 206–209, BEGZ10]. Only the dominating Kähler background enters this cohomological comparison; the nonclosed mass is recovered by smooth-background expansion and distributional Stokes. The two ordinary volumes and their divisor and pure-pullback laws are those of [Definition 3.1 and Proposition 3.3, BGL25] in their bounded-mass setting; here the latter identities are proved through the complete competitor correspondence, and the small-curvature sublogarithmic representatives give the extreme sequences. The ambient ideal orders of proposition 20.3.71 follow from a transverse radial integral. For proposition 20.3.74, the small-curvature criterion first produces a smooth residual representative; restriction to the last exceptional curve then excludes ordinary-type strictness even over pole centers. The exceptional curvature perturbation constructs a one-sided strict witness inductively. This extends the bounded-center restriction mechanism in example 10.17.9 to the specified finite blowup family. The separate residual volume and cost in 12.35.8 use the all-test dual formula and first variation of this book. The logarithmic degeneration in example 12.35.13 specializes those formulas to the height distribution on the sphere; pairing against a closed base test excludes every strict current at the endpoint.

25.11 Perspectives and further reading

25.11 Geometric problemsBCAE26692B2F

A closed strictly positive current has geometric consequences that a positive nonclosed background need not have, and this distinction governs the passage from the normalization of equations to the geometric criteria below. The characterization of Fujiki's class by Kähler currents used in section 24.4 is Demailly and Păun's [Theorem 0.7, DP04], and the transcendental Grauert–Riemenschneider conjecture is [Conjecture 0.8, DP04]; in the arXiv version of that paper these are Theorem 0.6 and Conjecture 0.7.

For nef classes with positive top self-intersection, the equivalence between bigness and bounded mass cited in section 24.4 is Guedj and Lu's [Theorem 4.9, GL22]. The characterization of Fujiki's class by bounded mass and positive upper volume of the class is [Theorem C, BGL25]; that upper volume is different from the Gauduchon functional for a fixed probability measure.

The transcendental Morse inequality for closed classes on compact Kähler manifolds, and its consequences for differentiability of the volume and duality of cones, mentioned in section 24.4, are Tosatti's [Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, version 2, Tosatti26]; they are quoted from the literature, and their proofs are not reproduced. The qualitative criterion under bounded mass is [Theorem 4.12, GL22].

The non-Hermitian locus in section 24.4 is that of Dang [Definition 2.12 and Theorem 2.14, DangNull26], where almost analytic singularities have the precise meaning of [Definition 2.8, DangNull26], including a smooth remainder on a suitable log resolution. Dang's qualitative identification of this locus with the null locus, for nef and big backgrounds that may be nonclosed, is [Theorem 1.1, DangNull26]. Theorem A of the same paper gives a numerical criterion under different hypotheses: bounded mass on the ambient manifold and positive lower volume on its submanifolds of positive dimension.

Theorem C of [DangNull26] identifies the singularities of the Chern–Ricci flow at a finite time with the null locus when the limiting lower volume is positive, for arbitrary initial metrics in dimension two and for initial metrics of Guan–Li type in higher dimensions, that is, initial metrics $\omega _0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega _0=0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega _0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega _0=0$. Once the limiting background is big, [Theorem 4.3, DangNull26] gives convergence as currents and smooth local convergence away from its non-Hermitian locus. This conditional parabolic input should be distinguished from the implication from positive volume to bigness without further hypotheses, which fails by theorem 12.34.10.

The theorem on the maximal existence time, theorem 12.34.4, is Tosatti and Weinkove's [Theorem 1.2, (1.4), and Section 4, arXiv version, TW15]. The proof given here combines the positive affine path and time-weighted estimates for the potential with lemma 14.5.1 and classical parabolic regularity. In the conversion to the book's conventions, potentials are multiplied by $2\pi $ and time is unchanged. The conditions for geometric smoothing in [Section 3.1, DNGL26] include the further compatibility discussed in section 25.8.

Distance estimates for a twisted flow also depend on its parameters. In Section 5.2 of [v2, p. 18, Dang26] the twist is fixed to be $\operatorname {Ric}(\omega _ X)$, for the reference metric $\omega _ X$ of that paper, and Theorem 5.7, p. 21, there allows the constants to depend on the endpoint of a finite time interval. The flat flows of example 12.34.14 show why the formulation for arbitrary twists in Theorem C of the introduction of that paper needs further control: a fixed initial density and a fixed lifetime do not bound the diameter independently of the twist, and a single positive twist can give unbounded diameter over an infinite lifetime.

The conjecture on balanced and pluriclosed metrics referred to in section 24.4 is stated by Fino and Vezzoni [Conjecture 1.1, FV26]; there the balanced and the pluriclosed metric are allowed to be different. That a compact manifold in Fujiki's class admitting a pluriclosed metric is Kähler is Chiose's [Theorem 0.2 in the author manuscript, Chiose14]; the locator refers to Chiose's manuscript version of that paper.

The case of parallel torsion, theorem 24.4.20, is a theorem of Chen and Zheng [v1, Theorem 1.2, pp. 2 and 8, CZParallel26]. Their projection by integration of parallel forms and their description of the holonomy are [v1, Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and Propositions 3.3–3.5, pp. 3–6, CZParallel26]; lemma 24.4.17 proves both descriptions again in a form that keeps track of positivity and of commutation with the differential. The slice of fixed trace and the maximum of the volume are [v1, Propositions 4.2 and 4.5, Lemmas 4.3–4.4, pp. 7–8, CZParallel26]. The inverse of the positive cofactor map proves the step of taking roots directly, and lemma 24.4.19 proves, by linear algebra of primitive forms, that a Hermitian form which is both balanced and pluriclosed is closed. The additional obstruction of Zhao and Zheng for non-balanced metrics with Bismut-parallel torsion, used in their Corollary 1.3, is a separate ingredient.

The conjectured long-time existence and convergence of the pluriclosed flow on balanced manifolds with $c_1(X)=0$ is [Conjecture 1.2, FV26]. The discussion in section 24.4 distinguishes a conserved balanced trace from a pointwise bound for the metric.

The persistence of pluriclosed metrics under deformations, theorem 24.4.28, which assumes that the Aeppli number $h_ A^{1,1}$ is constant, is Cavalcanti's [v5, Theorem 8.11, Section 8.3, pp. 41–42, CavSKT13]. The fourth-order Aeppli Laplacian and the realization of Aeppli classes by harmonic forms used in lemma 24.4.24 are due to Schweitzer [v1, Section 2.c, pp. 9–10, SchAeppli07], who constructs the elliptic symbol in Section 2.b, pp. 7–8. The proof given here writes the projection onto $\partial \bar\partial $-closed forms explicitly and obtains its smooth dependence on the parameter from the resolvent and the constancy of the dimension of the kernel. It applies to any finite-dimensional smooth parameter space and keeps the prescribed initial metric. This is also the analytic input stated in [v1, Theorem 2.1, p. 7, BarDef26]; Barbaro's construction of deformations of Lie groups there requires a separate argument with transverse cohomology.
